items.title: Index chat history into a vector store via a scheduled pipeline

milestone.title: Chat History & Recall
milestone.description: Users can easily see what they did and when, with search, filters and a timeline. Agents can answer questions about past conversations.

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
Chat conversations are reconstructed from the durable agent-event log (`PersistedAgentEventEntity` / `ThreadEntity`) and can only be found by thread name today (`name__icontains`). This issue builds the foundation for semantic search over chat history: a **scheduled Dagster pipeline** that periodically turns each conversation thread into a document — each `(user message, assistant response)` pair a chunk — embeds it, and writes it into a dedicated chat-history collection with metadata identifying the thread, participating agents, and users.

Chat history, distilled memory and RAG knowledge share one substrate: `PartitionAwareMilvusVectorStore` for writes, `KnowledgeRetriever` for reads, `NodeMetadata` for the schema, with the `origin` / `scope_*` axis established by #1716. Verbatim turns are distinguished from distilled facts and ingested documents by **metadata, not a parallel implementation**. Chat history gets its own Milvus collection because its retention and consent profile differs from documents — not because it needs its own code path.

This is **one fixed pipeline deployed once**, serving all threads. It has no per-knowledge-database axis, so it does not reintroduce the deploy-per-database coupling #1505 removes: no tenant, collection, or bucket may be baked into asset keys, partition names, resources, jobs, or NATS topics.

**In scope**

- A deployed Dagster pipeline (own code location, one deployment for all threads) that reads conversation threads from the agent-event log and reuses the pipeline package's document → chunk → embed → vector-store machinery. Each thread is one document; each user/assistant turn is one chunk.
- Runs on a schedule (~hourly), driven by per-thread version hashing: the first run indexes all existing threads (natural backfill — no separate migration), and each later run re-embeds only threads new or changed since the last run. No work on the live streaming/response path.
- A dedicated chat-history Milvus collection, written through `PartitionAwareMilvusVectorStore` and readable through `KnowledgeRetriever` with no chat-history-specific store wrapper or filter dialect.
- One namespace per user, matching the memory namespace layout from #1716, so partition pruning follows the way this index is actually queried (a user's own history). A thread with several participants is indexed once **per participant**, so each participant's namespace is self-contained and a user-scope search touches exactly one namespace.
- Chat turns carry `origin=chat_turn` plus per-chunk metadata filterable at query time: thread_id, participating agent_id(s)/agent_class(es), user_id(s), run_id/display_id, timestamp, and the source documents (knowledge database and `document_id`) the assistant's answer was grounded on, taken from the turn's retrieval events. A turn copied into another participant's namespace keeps the same references, since that participant may not be allowed to read those documents.
- Deletion propagates per user: deleting a thread drops that user's copy of the chunks. Other participants of a shared thread keep theirs, so an indexed conversation is never retrievable by a user who has deleted it.
- Whole-conversation retrieval by thread_id is preserved (via the event log and/or the per-thread document) so a caller can fetch an entire thread without semantic search.
- ADR: chat-history indexing as a scheduled pipeline (thread = document, turn = chunk), the collection and per-user namespace layout including per-participant duplication for shared threads, the per-user deletion-propagation guarantee, and the deliberate gap on chat-surface history clearing.

**Out of scope**

- The substrate conventions and the `origin` / `scope_*` metadata axis — established by #1716 (blocks this).
- The agent capability to query this index — see #1610 (sibling).
- The thread-admin semantic search UI — see #1611 (sibling).
- Distilled user/organization memory — see #1716 (blocks this); this issue indexes verbatim turns, not extracted facts.
- Purging the index when a user clears conversation history from a chat surface (e.g. the Teams `/removehistory` command). That command does not currently clear history at all — see #618 — so this is follow-up work once #618 is fixed. Until then, history cleared from a chat surface stays semantically searchable, which is a knowingly weaker privacy posture than thread deletion.
- Configurable retention windows / TTL-based purging. Deletion follows user action only; a retention policy is separate work.
- Hiding turns whose source documents the reading user may not read. Here they are only recorded; enforcement belongs with source permissions, see #2179.
- Graph or entity-relationship storage. Neo4j is not part of this substrate.

**Accepted when**

- [ ] A scheduled pipeline periodically indexes conversation threads into the chat-history collection — one document per thread, one chunk per user/assistant turn.
- [ ] Chat turns are written through `PartitionAwareMilvusVectorStore` and retrieved through `KnowledgeRetriever`, with no chat-history-specific store wrapper or filter dialect.
- [ ] Each chunk carries `origin=chat_turn`, its scope, and thread/participating-agent/user metadata, all filterable at query time.
- [ ] Each indexed assistant turn records the knowledge database and document of every source its answer was grounded on.
- [ ] The pipeline is deployed once and serves all threads, with no tenant, collection, or bucket baked into asset keys, partitions, resources, jobs, or NATS topics.
- [ ] The first run indexes the entire existing thread history; later runs re-embed only new or changed threads (via version hashing), with no work on the live response path.
- [ ] Deleting a thread removes the corresponding chunks from that user's namespace.
- [ ] A thread with multiple participants is retrievable by each of them, and one participant deleting it does not remove it for the others.
- [ ] The full conversation for a thread_id can be retrieved without semantic search.
- [ ] The design is recorded in an ADR.

---

**Blocked by #1716.**

items.title: [Feature]: Ability to use RLS with continuous aggregates, when the RLS rule matches the space partitioning key
items.body:
### What problem does the new feature solve?

**What problem does this feature solve**

One of the most popular (and most-suggested) ways of properly preventing data leakage in a multi-tenant SaaS architecture is to use row-level security (RLS). It's what my company does, and it's the only thing preventing us from adopting Timescale.

RLS already works with hypertables, but not with continuous aggregates. This prevents me from shipping awesome time-series dashboards to my users: my noisiest tables are full of samples from many customers, and need cached / materialized views to be performant.

**Alternatives Explored**

Alternative solutions are schema-per-tenant, database-per-tenant, or software-enforced isolation (or, I guess, don't use continuous aggregates - for us, the most valuable part of Timescale). 

I won't explain why schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant are heavier lift solutions; that topic is well trodden. They are the right choice for some cases, but not mine, and not for many others.

Software-enforced isolation is good enough for low-risk use cases, but constant code churn and frequent releases makes it possible for a software bug to slip in that could be potentially damaging to users' privacy, and therefore damaging to our company's ability to keep our users safe.

We made the decision that RLS is the right trade-off between convenience and security. It adds a layer of protection if a software bug might otherwise leak data, and it limits the blast radius from a hack.

### What does the feature do?

**What this feature would do**

This feature would make it possible to enable certain (see below) RLS policies on hypertables that are used in continuous aggregates.

### Implementation challenges

**Implementation challenges**

Since continuous aggregates need to maintain partial aggregate values in the materialization hypertable, it presents a challenge with RLS: The RLS policy can be arbitrarily complex, and would need to be applied at the level of the partial aggregate in order to carry through to the final, aggregated query results.

**Possible implementations**

1. Option 1 posits that it could be possible to enforce RLS policies on just the continuous aggregate view (NOT the source table). In this world, the user (me) is responsible for ensuring that the needed columns are on the materialization table. This would be super easy to implement as a user. I could add "tenant_id" to my "group by" clause. In my materialized view, there'd be separate aggregates for all my tenants. A simple RLS policy on the materialized view would ensure I don't accidentally show one tenant's data to another.
2. Option 2 is tricky. Since Timescale already supports distributed hypertables with continuous aggregates, it should be possible to enforce RLS policies that only rely on columns **that are used in the hypertable space partitioning**. In other words, if I have a distributed hypertable that is chunked on 2 columns, "create_date" and "tenant_id", **theoretically** I should be able to enforce RLS on "tenant_id". Presumably, the materialization hypertable includes the space partitioning key (at least, that's how I imagine it would work - I could be way off base here). And if the materialization hypertable has the data partitioned by tenant_id already, then I should be able to enforce RLS all the way through the pipeline.

I'm making a lot of assumptions about how Timescale works from the outside, but it seems to me that if space-partitioned distributed hypertables can support continuous aggregates, then RLS policies that only affect those same columns should be possible to get working as well.

I'd love feedback on either of these items. I still continue to champion Timescale in my company, but this feature is currently a deal-breaker for us.

Thanks for the awesome product and I hope to hear from you soon!

items.title: Validate native tenant store isolation
items.body:
Validate and document the blocker-independent native store selection portion of #38. Native-first inspection found that application-owned scoped `AddDbContext` factories and `PostgreSqlOutbox.BeginTransactionAsync(NpgsqlDataSource/Connection)` already select the transaction store. A library-owned resolver facade would duplicate those native configuration paths; record that decision rather than add a parallel API.

Scope:
- Exercise application-owned scoped store selection for manually initiated EF Core outbox units, with native Npgsql data sources and Relayer schema options.
- Exercise explicitly composed per-tenant EF Core consumer pipelines for isolated inbox/outbox transactions. These pipelines have a tenant known at composition; do not imply dynamic incoming-tenant selection works.
- Cover database-per-tenant and schema-per-tenant layouts without dynamic EF models or replacing native connection/pool configuration.
- Document native object ownership, authorization before resolving database services, unknown/missing tenant rejection, rollback, and the current dynamic-consumer limitation.

Acceptance criteria:
- Real PostgreSQL tests with several tenant databases and schemas prove business rows, overlapping inbox message IDs, outbox rows and rollback remain isolated.
- Concurrent application scopes resolve their selected native store independently; missing/unknown tenant selection never falls back to another store.
- Disposing application scopes/providers does not dispose application-owned shared Npgsql data sources.
- Website call sites use the actual existing APIs and identify application-owned selection types explicitly. Update the design/decision record to explain native factory reuse.

Dynamic TenantContext-to-database binding, removal of the consumer's startup tenant assumption, and automatic durable tenant/header consistency remain acceptance criteria of parent #38 after #264. Bounded dynamic dispatch remains #266. This issue can merge independently of #264; it does not mark multi-tenancy complete.

items.title: Audit 2026-10: architecture, scaling and quality review (overview and roadmap)

labels.name: priority: P1-high
labels.description: Blocks scaling to more tenants or real user pain

labels.name: source: audit-2026-10
labels.description: Found in the October 2026 architecture/security/UX audit

items.body:
Results of a multi-perspective review: an architecture/DevOps lead plus specialist reviews for Security, Architecture & multi-tenant scaling, UI/UX, Product, CI/CD, Testing and Code quality. **129 raw findings were deduplicated into 84 issues + 8 private security advisories**, grouped in 7 epics.

## Epics
- #93 Security remediation (**start here**; 8 private advisories)
- #95 Money correctness (billing, inventory, Kassen)
- #96 Delivery foundation: CI/CD, tests, environments, ops
- #94 Multi-tenant scaling & self-serve onboarding
- #97 UX for the bar, accessibility, design system
- #98 Code health & performance
- #99 Product roadmap
- #114 Full testing and strict code quality (wishlist)
- #115 Platform brand, Corps websites and custom design (wishlist)
- #116 Mobile apps, bar tablet and drinking features (wishlist)

## Owner wishlist (added 2026-10-26)
13 more issues (#101–#113) in three epics:
- **Testing and quality:** #101 full coverage with ratchet and mutation testing, #102 UI/a11y/visual tests, #103 strict Biome.
- **Brand and websites:** #105 platform brand and landing page, #104 websites for other Corps, #106 custom typeface and Couleur-band design language.
- **Apps and bar:** #108 bar tablet with personal PIN, #107 iOS/Android/tablet apps (Capacitor), #109 prepaid balance, #110 rounds, #111 low-stock alerts and barcode restocking, #112 event mode with guest tabs and live board, #113 stats and Semester Wrapped.

## Current architecture (as of 2026-10)
- **One Next.js 16 app on Vercel**, server actions as the API, `src/proxy.ts` as middleware.
- **Database per tenant (Turso/libSQL)** plus a **control-plane DB**, which holds tenants, domains, global Better Auth identity and sessions, memberships, feature flags, per-tenant Azure config and cross-Corps ELO. Users are mirrored into each tenant DB.
- Tenant is resolved from Host → `x-tenant-id` header. Most domain code uses an **implicit Proxy `db`** that routes each query by that header and falls back to the Rhenania DB outside a request.

**What's good:** DB-per-tenant is the right isolation model for clubs that handle money and personal data. It's cheap on Turso, gives per-tenant backup/restore and deletion, and the stateless HTTP clients scale to hundreds of tenants per instance. Feature flags and superadmin provisioning are a sound start.

## What breaks as you add tenants
| | 2 tenants (today) | ~10 | ~50 | ~200 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Authorization** | Rests on proxy path rules and hidden buttons; many server actions unguarded (#93) | every new Corps admin is a new attacker against all others | — | — |
| **Onboarding** | dev runs CLI scripts, redeploys for OAuth/domains (#27, #29) | ~1 day of dev time per Corps | not feasible | — |
| **Rhenania identity** | personal IBAN/address and legal pages served to Hassia (#9, #31) | legal risk per tenant | | |
| **Migrations** | laptop script, journal drift, repair scripts (#28, #43, #44) | mixed schemas after partial runs | rollout takes long and is unobservable | needs bounded parallel fan-out + versions |
| **Control DB load** | 3–10 round trips per request, `auth()` not memoized, 20 s polling that writes (#20, #21) | fine | control DB is the hot spot & SPOF | needs cookie cache + config cache |
| **Config consistency** | 5 per-instance caches, local-only invalidation (#30) | confusing flag/domain lag | support load | |
| **Secrets** | plaintext, never-expiring full-access tokens; Azure secrets expire ≤24 months (#38) | | a rotation every ~2 weeks | must be automated |
| **Ops** | no CI, no staging, dev = prod, no error tracking, no backups runbook (#96) | | blind to per-tenant failures | |

## Target architecture
1. **Authorize in the action, not the path.** `defineAction({schema, permission, feature}, fn)` wrapper: zod parse → `requirePermission` (membership in the current tenant + permission) → service call → typed result (#59, #92). The proxy only does tenant resolution and UX redirects.
2. **One request context** (`React.cache`): tenant, session (Better Auth cookie cache), membership and permissions resolved once per request (#20).
3. **Explicit tenant scope:** `src/server/modules/<domain>/{actions,service,repo}.ts`. Services take a `TenantScope`, and the implicit Proxy `db` and its prod fallback are retired (#33). Pure, unit-tested domain logic for money and inventory with integer cents (#58, #13).
4. **Permissions, not role names:** stable permission keys mapped to tenant-defined roles (#32).
5. **Versioned tenant config service:** host map, status, flags, branding, legal profile and auth config with `configVersion` invalidation. Secrets encrypted at rest. Auth providers resolved per request, so no redeploys (#30, #27, #38).
6. **Provisioning as a resumable state machine**, ending in a working first admin, domain, payment config and legal profile (#29, #60).
7. **Migrations from CI:** checks → canary → bounded-parallel fan-out → per-tenant schema version → deploy (expand/contract) (#28).
8. **Tenant-tagged observability + health view** (#34, #48), **staging/preview with isolated DBs, local dev on `file:` DBs** (#47, #46), **backups/DR** (#49).

Nothing here needs a rewrite or a new database model. It can all be done incrementally on the current stack.

## Suggested order
1. **This week:** fix the security advisories in #93 (ADV1/ADV2 are small), merge the Next/Better Auth security updates (#39), and fix the personal IBAN/address fallback (#9).
2. **Next 2–4 weeks:** CI + `pnpm check` green + local `file:` DBs + test harness (#41, #42, #46, #54, #92), then the money bugs in #95.
3. **Then:** request context and permissions, tenant config and auth without redeploys, provisioning workflow, release pipeline with migrations, legal/branding per tenant.
4. **Continuously:** UX for `/trinken` and the design system (#97), product roadmap (#99).

## Label guide
| Prefix | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `type:` | bug · feature · enhancement · refactor · chore · security · performance · docs · test · epic |
| `area:` | domain or technical area (billing, getraenke, multi-tenancy, auth, ci-cd, ui-ux, …) |
| `priority:` | **P0-critical** fix now (security, money, data loss) · **P1-high** blocks scaling or real user pain · **P2-medium** · **P3-low** |
| `effort:` | **S** < 1 day · **M** 1–3 days · **L** ~1–2 weeks · **XL** multi-week, should be split |
| `status:` | **agent-ready**: spec is clear enough for a coding agent · **needs-input**: open questions for the owner (see "Open questions" in the issue) · **needs-design**: needs a UX decision or mockup · **blocked** |
| `source: audit-2026-10` | created by this audit |

Find agent work with `label:"status: agent-ready" label:"priority: P1-high"`. Once you answer an issue's open questions, swap `status: needs-input` for `status: agent-ready`.

items.title: Tenant deployment orchestrator: versioned releases, migrations, and control-plane reconciliation

milestone.description: Everything that must ship before the authhero 1.0 release. Anything that can wait goes in a later milestone.

items.body:
## Context

WFP dispatch namespaces version user Workers internally but expose no versions API — no list, fetch, deploy-specific, or rollback ([confirmed in CF docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-for-platforms/workers-for-platforms/reference/limits/): "Gradual Deployments is not supported yet for user Workers. Changes made to user Workers create a new version that deployed all-at-once to 100% of traffic"). The public surface is script get/put/delete, content, settings, secrets, bindings, tags. "Changing a version" for a tenant means re-PUTting the bundle we want. Therefore we own the release registry, and per-tenant version management becomes a control-plane feature — which is also a product differentiator (per-tenant pinning / maintenance windows, something Auth0 doesn't offer).

Prior art reviewed: Atlas (atlasgo) database-per-tenant guides (target groups, drift detection, plan/apply, content-hashed migration dirs) and Turso Multi-DB Schemas (since deprecated). No off-the-shelf tool covers WFP code-version orchestration — every WFP platform builds its own control plane.

## Relationship to #1026 (already shipped)

This is **the next phase on the existing tenant-operations engine**, not a new system. Shipped via PRs #1037–#1040, #1042:

- `tenant_operations` + `tenant_operation_events` + `rollouts` control-plane tables (`packages/drizzle/src/schema/control-plane/`), with `target_worker_version` / `target_database_version`, canary tenant ids, wave size
- Executor adapter (`inline` | `cloudflare-workflows`), row-first enqueue, idempotent steps
- `createWfpProvisionerSteps` (packages/cloudflare): DB create → migrations → script PUT → secrets → seed → verify → mark-ready, already schema-first
- Tenant columns: `deployment_type`, `storage_kind`, `bundle_configuration`, `worker_version`, `database_version`, `worker_script_name`, `d1_database_id`
- Per-tenant D1 migration tracking table `_authhero_provisioner_migrations` (name + applied_at, legacy backfill handling)

**Genuinely new in this issue:** release registry (R2 + `releases`/`channels` tables), build-time `requires_schema` derivation, the `upgrade` operation steps (kind exists in the enum, no executor steps yet), drift detection, write-freeze, and the reconciliation loop.

## Design

**Model: desired state + reconciliation** (operator pattern). Directory DB holds desired state per tenant; controllers diff against observed state and converge. Every fleet operation produces a reviewable plan before apply (canary tenants first via `rollouts`, fail-fast per tenant).

**Release registry**
- CI publishes immutable artifacts to R2: `releases/{project}/{semver}/worker.mjs` + `manifest.json`
- Release version = the consuming project's semver (the deployable artifact), with authhero package versions recorded in the manifest as provenance
- Manifest also carries bindings, compatibility_date, compatibility_flags — a code rollback re-PUTs matching config, not just matching JS
- `requires_schema` derived at build time from the bundled adapter's Drizzle migration journal head — no manual bookkeeping (same derivation as today's `database_version` = last migration name)
- Everything content-hashed; verify before apply

**Directory schema (control plane)**
- `releases` (version, r2_key, git_sha, schema_head, channel, created_at) — new
- `channels` (stable/beta → version) — new
- tenant rows: reuse existing `deployment_type` (pooled/shared vs dedicated/wfp) and `storage_kind` (engine); add `channel` + optional `pinned_version` (two columns, not one polymorphic ref) + write-freeze flag. `worker_version` / `database_version` remain the observed state.
- Per-migration observability: reuse `tenant_operation_events` (step = migration name) rather than a new `migration_attempts` table

**Deploy sequence per tenant (durable workflow — extends `createWfpProvisionerSteps` into the `upgrade` operation)**
1. Resolve desired release (pin or channel)
2. Check `requires_schema` vs tenant `database_version`
3. Apply pending migrations via D1 HTTP batch — **migration SQL and its `_authhero_provisioner_migrations` insert in the same batch** (today they're separate calls; a crash between them re-runs non-idempotent DDL), one migration per batch; record attempts as operation events
4. PUT worker bundle + metadata (bindings/flags from manifest) to dispatch namespace script; secrets re-synced (upgrade must not drop them)
5. Mirror state onto script tags (`version:x.y.z`, `channel:stable`, `tenant:id`) as out-of-band drift check (8-tag limit per script; 2 already used by the provisioner)
6. Post-deploy verify step (health check against the tenant) before marking succeeded
7. Update directory

**Rules**
- Schema first, code second. Forward-only migrations, expand/contract discipline (every migration backward-compatible with the **oldest supported pinned version**, not just the previous release; destructive cleanup ships N releases later). Rollback = code only, never schema.
- **Version-skew policy**: pinning is bounded by a support window (max N releases behind the channel head). Pins older than the window block destructive migrations fleet-wide, so pins need expiry/escalation. Pinned tenants' schemas advance only when their deployed release's `requires_schema` demands it.
- **Per-tenant single-flight**: at most one running operation per tenant (lease or conditional status transition on `tenant_operations`). The current engine's idempotent steps don't prevent a rollout wave and a reconciler converging the same tenant concurrently.
- One migration system owns any given database. Pooled plane = Kysely/PlanetScale (single shared DB, single migration run). Dedicated plane = Drizzle/D1, tracked via `_authhero_provisioner_migrations` (the Drizzle journal is a build-time input only — no second tracking table on tenant DBs).
- Feature parity enforced via the shared adapter conformance suite, not schema identity.
- Worker schema-compatibility check: primary enforcement is the post-deploy verify step in the workflow. The runtime check is a cached backstop that serves a maintenance response — **not** a cold-start crash loop (that turns a control-plane mistake into a hard tenant outage and adds a D1 read per cold start).
- Write-freeze enforcement mechanism must be explicit (request-time check against pushed config, not just a directory flag).

**Drift detection**: background scan comparing script tags, `_authhero_provisioner_migrations`, and config hashes against directory; flag (not auto-fix) anything changed outside the pipeline. Directory is truth; tags are a hint (a PUT can succeed while the tag update fails). Drizzle's per-migration snapshots give schema-drift diffing nearly free.

**Future controllers on the same engine** (same desired/observed/plan/apply contract): config push (config lives in tenant DB, controller pushes diffs), backup policy (check D1 Time Travel first; build long-retention R2 export on top), log routing config (reconcile the routing, not the stream — logs stay on the tail-worker/OTLP path). Pool→dedicated extraction workflow (filter by tenant_id, transform MySQL→SQLite, verify hashes, flip routing, delete from pool) as a later controller — sessions/refresh tokens must migrate or tenant users get logged out.

## Open decisions

- [ ] WFP-per-tenant vs cell Workers: per-tenant version pinning is the strongest argument for WFP; partly pre-decided by the shipped `deployment_type` column — revisit explicitly before adding `releases`/`channels` columns
- [ ] Pooled plane: permanent standard tier vs transitional (determines whether we invest in extraction workflow or in dual-schema authoring ergonomics)
- [ ] Version-skew window size (how many releases behind a pin may fall) and pin expiry/escalation policy
- [ ] Verify email/collation semantics in the D1 Drizzle schema before migrating real tenants (MySQL CI collation vs SQLite case sensitivity — login-lookup risk)
- [ ] Confirm D1 Time Travel coverage before building backup exports

## Non-goals (for now)
- Down migrations across the fleet
- Generic framework / UI — one workflow engine, controllers added when a real task exists
- Gradual (percentage) rollout within a single tenant (not supported by WFP user Workers anyway)

items.title: Multi-tenant architecture: support per-client GCP environments for managed hosting

labels.name: qa-gate-post-mvp
labels.description: Findings from the Post-MVP QA Gate verification checkpoint

items.body:
**Source:** Strategic architectural concern raised by Franz during the Post-MVP QA Gate (2026-04-08).

## Current state

The codebase assumes a **single GCP project** for all data and services. \`mulder.config.yaml\` has exactly one \`gcp.project_id\` field, all repository writes target one bucket / one Cloud SQL instance / one Firestore database. \`packages/core/src/shared/services.gcp.ts:371\` builds a single \`Services\` object from one config — there is no notion of \"which client / which tenant am I serving right now\".

This is fine for the current open-source MVP that you self-host, but it blocks two future scenarios:

1. **Side-by-side projects.** Franz already has two distinct domains in flight (the UFO archive that this code was built for, and the IGAAP project). They should be **isolated by GCP project**, not multiplexed inside one.
2. **Managed hosting offering.** If the system proves itself, hosting it as a managed service for paying clients becomes a viable business model. Clients must be isolated from each other:
   - Separate billing
   - Separate IAM (no client A admin can read client B documents)
   - Separate Cloud SQL instance (or at least separate database with row-level isolation, but a separate instance is simpler and more defensible)
   - Separate GCS buckets
   - Independent quota/rate limits

## Why P2 (not P0/P1)

This is a **strategic feature**, not a bug. The MVP works correctly for one project today. There is no immediate failure mode being fixed — only future flexibility being added.

But it should be **planned now** because:
- The Terraform module work (planned for M8 / I3, currently the empty \`terraform/\` directory referenced in #100 / P6-DOCS-CLAUDE-01) is the natural place to introduce the multi-tenant primitives. Doing it twice would be wasteful.
- The config schema cannot be evolved later without a breaking change for existing self-hosted users — better to design \`gcp\` as a multi-tenant-friendly nested object now and have a single-tenant default than to refactor in M9.
- The IGAAP onboarding pressure is real: Franz needs an isolated environment for that project NOW, not after the managed-hosting launch.

## GCP primitives that solve this

GCP offers three layers of multi-tenancy, each with different cost/complexity:

| Layer | What it isolates | Complexity | Best for |
|-------|------------------|------------|----------|
| **Folders + Projects** | Billing, IAM, all resources | Low | The right answer here. Each client/tenant = one GCP Project, grouped under a Folder. |
| **Organization** | Org-level policies, security perimeters | Medium | Multi-folder hierarchies; needed once you have ≥10 clients |
| **VPC Service Controls** | Network-level data perimeter | High | Compliance-driven (HIPAA, SOC2) — overkill until a client demands it |

**Recommended path:** Folder-per-tier (e.g. \`mulder-clients/\`), one GCP Project per tenant inside that folder. Terraform takes a \`tenant_id\` input variable and provisions a complete isolated environment.

## Acceptance criteria (epic-level)

This issue is an **epic** — it should spawn sub-issues during M8 design. At a minimum:

- [ ] **Config schema** evolved: \`gcp\` becomes either (a) a tenant-keyed map, or (b) the env var \`MULDER_TENANT_ID\` selects which \`gcp\` block to load. Pick one — option (b) is simpler for the CLI.
- [ ] **Terraform module** \`terraform/modules/tenant\` that takes \`tenant_id\`, \`billing_account\`, \`folder_id\` and provisions: GCP Project, Cloud SQL instance, GCS bucket, Document AI processor, Firestore database, IAM bindings.
- [ ] **\`mulder tenant create <id>\`** CLI command that runs the Terraform module + writes a per-tenant config file under \`~/.mulder/tenants/{id}.yaml\`.
- [ ] **\`mulder --tenant <id>\`** flag (or \`MULDER_TENANT_ID\` env var) that selects which tenant's config to load.
- [ ] **Cross-tenant isolation test:** ingest two PDFs into two tenants, query each, verify zero cross-pollination at the DB and GCS level.
- [ ] **Billing labels:** every GCP resource provisioned by the Terraform module carries \`tenant_id\` as a label, so the billing export can break down costs per tenant.
- [ ] **Documentation:** README \"Self-host\" section shows the single-tenant case (current behavior); \"Managed offering\" section (new) shows multi-tenant.

## Dependencies and ordering

- **Blocked by:** #100 (the \`terraform/\` directory does not even exist yet — that gap must be closed first)
- **Blocks:** Any \"managed offering\" go-live; the IGAAP onboarding (which currently has to share infrastructure with the UFO archive)
- **Should land in:** M8 (Operations) — this is exactly the kind of operational concern M8 was designed for

## Open questions for design phase

1. **Single org vs multi-org?** A single mulder-platform org with folders per client is cheaper but couples client billing to your top-level account. A separate org per client is fully decoupled but requires each client to create their own Google Workspace org (high friction).
2. **Shared vs dedicated Document AI processors?** Processors carry per-call cost and a quota. Sharing one processor across tenants is cheaper but mixes telemetry; dedicating one per tenant is cleaner but costs ~€10/month/tenant in idle quota.
3. **Cloud SQL: instance per tenant vs database per tenant on a shared instance?** Instance-per-tenant is the strongest isolation (also matches \"sovereign data\" stories) but costs ~€30/month per idle tenant. Database-per-tenant on one instance is ~80% cheaper but introduces a noisy-neighbor risk.
4. **Cost model for the managed offering:** flat per-tenant fee, per-document fee, or both?

## Why this becomes an issue now (and not later)

Phase 4 of the QA Gate ran the entire pipeline against the current single-project setup and produced finding **P4-GCP-DOCAI-REGION-01** (#93). Fixing #93 means touching \`services.gcp.ts:371-419\` — the same function that would need to take a \`tenantId\` parameter in the multi-tenant world. **It is half the work to do both at once** vs. fixing #93 now and refactoring again later.

## See also

- #93 Document AI region — same code area
- #100 Docs drift — terraform/ gap that must close before this can land
- \`docs/reviews/post-mvp-gcp-smoketest.md\` §1 (current GCP environment)

items.title: Multi-tenancy
Newly-created Cloud DB returns `SERVER_ERROR: Server returned HTTP status 404` for ~2.5s after the Platform API reports it exists (create→serve gap, no readiness signal)
items.body:
## Summary

A query to a **freshly-created Turso Cloud database** throws `LibsqlError: SERVER_ERROR: Server returned HTTP status 404` for **~2.5 seconds after the Platform API has acknowledged the create and the control plane reports the database as existing**. There is no readiness signal to wait on, and the 404 is **byte-identical** to the one a database that never existed returns — so it's indistinguishable from "database not found".

This is the natural sequel to #189 ("Confusing error message when database URL does not exist"): the same `404` is *also* returned for a database that **does** exist but whose libSQL endpoint isn't serving yet.

The root cause looks platform-side (control plane vs. data plane), but it surfaces entirely through `@libsql/client`, and there's a concrete client-side ask below, so filing here — happy to move if there's a better tracker.

## Environment

- `@libsql/client` 0.17.3, Node v22.22.0
- Turso Cloud, database-per-database in a group (created via Platform API `POST /v1/organizations/{org}/databases`)
- Reproduced both **in-region** (Vercel `iad1` ↔ `aws-us-east-1` group) and **cross-region** (see Region below)

## The error

```
LibsqlError: SERVER_ERROR: Server returned HTTP status 404
  (cause: HttpServerError, status 404)
```

## Reproduction

Minimal, self-contained, secrets-free: **https://github.com/ejc3/turso-create-serve-404**

```sh
npm install
TURSO_API_TOKEN=… TURSO_ORG=… TURSO_GROUP=… TURSO_GROUP_AUTH_TOKEN=… node repro.mjs
```

For each fresh db it samples **both planes against one clock**, and queries the data plane both at *control-exists* (`data@control`) and **after the create `POST` returned 200 to the caller** (`data@post-ack`). Reproduces 6/6–10/10 every run; each db is deleted afterward:

```
baseline: data-plane query to a NEVER-created db → 404  (same HTTP 404 as the create→serve case)

# 1 reprotest-a483aa0d: POST-ack@465ms | control "exists"@144ms → data@control=404 | data@post-ack=404 | data serves@2504ms | gap=2360ms  ← create→serve 404
# 2 reprotest-ec2257b2: POST-ack@399ms | control "exists"@124ms → data@control=404 | data@post-ack=404 | data serves@2458ms | gap=2334ms  ← create→serve 404
# 4 reprotest-f2b422cc: POST-ack@326ms | control "exists"@226ms → data@control=404 | data@post-ack=404 | data serves@2447ms | gap=2221ms  ← create→serve 404
...
RESULT: 6/6 reproduced the create→serve 404 (data plane 404'd at control-exists and/or after POST-ack, AND the db later served)
gap (control "exists" → data serves): min=2189ms median=2342ms max=2360ms
```

A reproduction is counted **only** when the data plane 404s **and the same database later serves** — so wrong credentials / permanent unavailability cannot be a false positive.

## Mechanism (and why it is NOT a client read-before-write)

Sampling both planes from one `t0` (just before the create `POST`):

| signal | when |
|---|---|
| control plane `GET /databases/{name}` first returns `200` ("exists") | **~75–230ms** |
| `POST /databases` returns `200` to the caller (create ACKed) | ~260–470ms |
| a data-plane `SELECT 1` at the instant the control plane said "exists" (`data@control`) | **`404`** |
| a data-plane `SELECT 1` **after the `POST` returned 200 to the caller** (`data@post-ack`) | **`404`** |
| the data-plane endpoint first actually serves | **~2.4–2.6s** |
| **gap (control "exists" → data serves)** | **~2.2–2.5s** |

Two independent witnesses rule out "the client queried before its write landed":

1. **`data@control`** runs *after* the control plane confirmed the db exists — Turso has durably registered the create — yet the data plane 404s.
2. **`data@post-ack`** runs *after `POST /databases` returned 200 to the caller* — the write call has demonstrably completed for the client — and it **still** 404s for ~2s more.

In both cases the **same hostname + same credentials** 404s and then serves with no change on the caller's side. That is a control→data serve/propagation gap inside Turso.

And per the `baseline` line: a query to a never-created database returns the **same HTTP 404**, so the error alone can't distinguish "not ready yet" from "doesn't exist" (cf. #189).

## Region

- **Cross-region** (client outside the group's region): gap ~2.2–2.5s (table above).
- **In-region** (Vercel `iad1` against an `aws-us-east-1` group): the control plane reports "exists" within ~20ms; the gap is shorter but **still reliably hit** — a fan-out of cold readers that connect at the "exists" signal saw **62/80** queries `404` across **7/8** fresh databases in `iad1`.

The window exists in- and cross-region; it's merely larger the farther the reader is from the group.

## Impact

The database-per-tenant / per-session / per-agent pattern (which Turso Cloud is marketed for) creates a fresh database on the hot path. Any reader that connects based on the control plane's "exists" signal — a separate process, a cold serverless instance, a second request — lands in this window and 404s on the first query of a brand-new database.

## Suggested fixes (any one helps)

1. **A readiness signal** — expose database status (`provisioning` → `ready`) on the Platform API, or don't let `GET /databases/{name}` return `200` until the data-plane endpoint serves.
2. **Make the not-ready response unambiguous** — return a distinct, retryable status/code (e.g. `425`/`409`/a `provisioning` error) instead of a bare `404` that collides with "does not exist". (This part is actionable in `@libsql/client`: surface a distinct error type for the not-ready/404 case so callers can retry without string-matching.)
3. **Make `POST /databases` not ACK until the endpoint serves** (synchronous create), so create completion *is* the readiness signal.

## Current workaround

After opening a connection to a freshly-created database, probe `SELECT 1` with bounded exponential backoff, retrying **only** the 404 / unresolved-host transients, before treating the connection as usable. It reliably absorbs the window — but it's a guess at an opaque, unbounded delay that a readiness signal would make unnecessary.

items.body:
**Parent epic:** #5 (ORGANIZE: Unified Data Model & Entity Profiles)
**Iteration:** Iteration 3 (due Nov 3, 2026) · part of Release 1 (Iteration 4, due Nov 17, 2026)
**Story points:** 5

## Goal
Make it impossible for one client's data to reach another client, and prove it on every PR.

## Context
Decision D5: `tenant_id` on every table, enforced in the query layer, proven by a CI test. This is the Law 25 boundary between clients. One database per tenant stays a future upgrade path.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] A tenant-scoped data access layer (repositories or a session bound to a tenant) used by all application code; every query is filtered by `tenant_id` automatically (#143: `TenantSession` and `bound_to_tenant` in `app/core/tenancy.py`)
- [x] Code cannot query a tenant-owned table without a tenant context; doing so raises an error (`TenantContextError`)
- [x] Raw SQL outside the data access layer is not allowed, and a lint rule or test flags it (`tests/test_data_access.py`)
- [x] Cross-tenant isolation test: with data for tenants A and B, every repository method and API endpoint called as tenant A returns nothing of tenant B, including by guessing B's ids (`tests/integration/test_tenant_isolation.py`, `test_tenancy.py`)
- [x] The isolation test runs in CI on every PR (#18) (Backend tests job; making it a required check is the branch protection item on #18)
- [x] Wiki page "Tenancy" explains the rule and how to add a new table safely ([Tenancy](https://github.com/antholim/Pulse/wiki/Tenancy))

## Tasks
- [x] Implement the tenant context and scoped session
- [x] Implement the repositories (session-bound scope instead, as the acceptance criteria allow)
- [x] Write the isolation test
- [x] Add it to CI
- [x] Write the wiki page

## Dependencies
- **Blocked by:** #18 Set up CI pipeline on every push and pull request, #25 Implement data model v1 with tenant_id on every table
- **Blocks:** #63 Expose a tenant-scoped REST API for organizations, sync runs and changes

## Out of scope
- Users, login and roles (#10)
- One database per tenant

## Rubric coverage
`Code: Security strategy and implementation of practices` · `Code: Tests` · `Code: Using best practices for framework`

## Definition of done
- [x] Acceptance criteria met
- [x] PR reviewed by at least one teammate and linked with `Closes #<this issue>` (#143)
- [x] CI green (lint, tests, coverage)
- [x] Wiki updated

items.title: Fivetran lineage binds same-named tables to the first service in dbServiceNames
items.body:
### Connector

Fivetran

### Feature area

Lineage

### Describe the bug

When several services in `lineageInformation.dbServiceNames` hold a table with the same database, schema and name, the Fivetran connector attaches every connector's lineage to the first listed service.

`_resolve_table` in `pipeline/fivetran/metadata.py` loops over `dbServiceNames` in order and returns the first service where `<service>.<database or *>.<schema>.<table>` exists. It never uses which source the Fivetran connector actually reads from. Sharded or per-tenant estates, where several databases share one schema, are the common case.

In our instance six MySQL services hold the same `evo` schema, one per Fivetran connector. With all six in one agent's `dbServiceNames`, all six connectors' 273 table edges were attached to the first service. Nothing was logged and the run reported success.

### To Reproduce

1. Two database services, A and B, each with table `db.schema.t`.
2. Two Fivetran connectors, one syncing from A and one from B.
3. A Fivetran agent with `dbServiceNames: [A, B]`.
4. Both connectors' lineage originates from A.

### Expected behavior

The source service is chosen from the Fivetran connector's own source (for example its configured host, or its database/service type), or the ambiguity is reported and the edge skipped rather than bound to the first match.

Our workaround is one Fivetran agent per source service, each with a `pipelineFilterPattern` and only its own service in `dbServiceNames`.

### OS

Kubernetes (ingestion-base image)

### Python version

3.12

### OpenMetadata version

2.0.6

### OpenMetadata Ingestion package version

openmetadata-ingestion==2.0.1.0; same logic on main.

### Pre-submission checklist

- [x] I searched for duplicate issues.
- [x] I removed credentials, hostnames, emails, and other sensitive data from logs and config.

items.title: Closed set of document types and attributes extracted at ingestion

labels.name: data-extraction
labels.description: Document Tables / extract_records roadmap: every ticket of the data extraction effort

labels.name: extraction:2-selection
labels.description: Data extraction step 2/4: dates in paths, document types and attributes at ingest

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
Agents that pick documents from a knowledge database can only filter by path and text today. A closed set of document types, each with a fixed list of attributes extracted once at ingestion, lets them select documents reliably instead of guessing from paths or reading every document. Ingestion currently stores file timestamps, title and language, but not what a document is or its business attributes, such as the date on an invoice or the parties of a contract. The set is closed on purpose: a filter over a fixed vocabulary is reliable, an open set the model invents per document is not.

**In scope**

- Define the set: about ten document types common in enterprise knowledge (for example invoice, contract, offer, delivery note, letter, meeting minutes, report, policy, other), and for each type the attributes worth extracting (for example document date, period covered, counterparty, reference number). Working out and justifying this list is part of the issue.
- A step in the default ingestion pipeline that classifies each document into one type and extracts that type's attributes from its opening pages with one small-model call.
- Type and attributes stored on the document record and as filterable metadata in the vector store.
- An attribute the model cannot determine with confidence is stored empty, never guessed.
- A backfill for documents that are already ingested.

**Out of scope**

- Agents filtering by these attributes, see #2348.
- Custom types or attributes per tenant or per knowledge database; the set is closed for now.
- Choosing the model per knowledge database, see #1782.

**Planning decisions**

- Invoices first: the set starts as `invoice` or `other`, measured on the 106 invoices of #2312 before further types follow (#2485).
- Invoice attributes: issue date, invoice number, issuer, issuer tax ID, recipient, parties, total amount including VAT, currency, due date, service period and the numbers of related documents. Addresses, bank details, line items and tax breakdowns are left out: they are not filters, and line items are read at request time.
- Attributes are shared across types, each type lists the ones that apply and what they mean for it, and one primary type owns them while secondary types are labels only.
- The model copies values as written; code converts them to one stored form and keeps the original text, so a better parser can fill values later without a model call. A value not found in the document, or not applicable to the type, is stored empty.
- The values are filter metadata only: they stay out of embedded and model-facing text, so embeddings never change and a backfill never embeds again.
- Classification uses the knowledge database's own text model and is switched per database, on by default. A failed call leaves the document unclassified instead of failing ingestion.
- Names of people on invoices are stored like any other value: the PII guardrail keeps data from leaving the platform, not from being stored inside it.
- Targets agreed by the team: invoice recall of at least 95%, precision on documents resembling invoices of at least 95%, and wrong plus guessed values at most 2% per attribute, measured with the PII guardrail on.

**Sub-issues, one stacked PR each, merged in this order**

#2480 classifier and storage contract → #2481 evaluation → #2482 ingestion → #2483 backfill → #2484 UI request. #2485 extends the set beyond invoices after the evaluation.

> **spike-tenant-ef-core-isolation** · Research spike · part of #76

> The text between the `board-ticket:source` markers below is the source of truth for the pipeline (`board fetch` reads it back verbatim). Edit it there; everything outside the markers is generated.

<!-- board-ticket:source:begin -->
# Spike: EF Core Tenant Isolation (Finbuckle.MultiTenant Compared With a Custom Implementation)

## Question

How should eShop enforce per-tenant data isolation in a shared database per service, given
the decision to use EF Core global query filters only (no PostgreSQL row-level security)?

## Why

Query filters are the only line of defence, so the mechanism must be hard to get wrong. It
must:

- apply the filter to every `ITenantOwned` entity automatically;
- set `TenantId` on save;
- block changes to `TenantId`;
- make skipping the filter explicit and easy to audit.

## Investigate

- **Finbuckle.MultiTenant** (`MultiTenantDbContext`, `IsMultiTenant()`, tenant stores and
  resolution strategies) compared with a small custom implementation (an `ITenantOwned`
  convention, a `SaveChangesInterceptor`, and a model-building convention that adds
  `HasQueryFilter`). Compare:
  - fit with Aspire and `AddNpgsqlDbContext`;
  - DbContext pooling;
  - the compiled model;
  - migrations;
  - testability.
- **Query filters in EF Core 10:** named filters, whether several filters on one entity
  combine, and how `IgnoreQueryFilters` behaves.
- **DbContext pooling:** how the tenant reaches a pooled context safely (`ITenantContext`
  captured per request, not per context instance).
- **Raw SQL and Dapper paths** in the existing services (for example Ordering queries) that
  skip the filters, and how to cover them.
- **Architecture tests** (NetArchTest or Roslyn analyzers) that fail when:
  - an entity with a `TenantId` property doesn't implement `ITenantOwned`;
  - `IgnoreQueryFilters()` is used outside the allow-listed namespace.
- **Backfill migration pattern** for existing tables (AdventureWorks GUID default, then
  non-null, then indexes).

## Deliverable

A recommendation with a small proof of concept on one DbContext, the chosen library or custom
design, and the architecture-test approach. Feeds TENANT-1 and TENANT-5.
<!-- board-ticket:source:end -->

items.title: [ARCH-04] PostgreSQL Persistence, Tenant Isolation and Schema Evolution
items.body:
## Architecture implementation ticket

This architecture ticket is binding across the StrataAI2 functional PRDs.

### Adopted StrataAI2 override
Use PostgreSQL as the primary datastore, PostgreSQL RLS as defence in depth, **pgvector** for semantic retrieval, and ordered versioned migrations. PostgreSQL also hosts transactional outbox/job metadata initially. Do not add MongoDB, Elasticsearch, or a separate vector database without measured need and an ADR.

# ARCH-04 — PostgreSQL Persistence, Tenant Isolation and Schema Evolution

## 1. PRD identifier
ARCH-04

## 2. Feature name
PostgreSQL Persistence, Tenant Isolation and Schema Evolution

## 3. Executive summary
Use PostgreSQL through Npgsql with application tenant checks and PostgreSQL RLS as defence in depth, while adding disciplined versioned migrations for the larger product.

## 4. Problem statement
The expanded StrataAI functional suite requires a stable architecture contract. Without one, teams or coding agents could choose incompatible frameworks, data-access patterns, security boundaries, runtime modes, or release mechanisms.

## 5. Product objective
Provide durable multi-Organization persistence that cannot leak data across tenants and can evolve safely through CI and deployment.

## 6. User personas
- Software developer
- Technical architect
- DevOps/release engineer
- Security/privacy reviewer
- System administrator
- Quality engineer

## 7. User stories
- As a developer, I know exactly where this capability belongs and which interfaces it must use.
- As a release engineer, I can reproduce the same build locally and in CI.
- As a security reviewer, I can identify the trust and tenant boundaries.
- As an operator, I can run, diagnose, upgrade, and roll back the application.

## 8. Functional requirements
- **ARCH-04-FR-001** — Production SHALL use PostgreSQL 17+ through Npgsql.
- **ARCH-04-FR-002** — Every tenant-owned table SHALL carry a non-null `tenant_id`/Organization isolation key unless demonstrably global.
- **ARCH-04-FR-003** — Every tenant-owned production query SHALL require explicit tenant context.
- **ARCH-04-FR-004** — PostgreSQL RLS SHALL be enabled and forced on tenant-owned tables where technically applicable.
- **ARCH-04-FR-005** — Database access SHALL set transaction-local/application-local tenant context before RLS-protected operations.
- **ARCH-04-FR-006** — Missing/malformed/unauthorized tenant context SHALL fail closed.
- **ARCH-04-FR-007** — Schema evolution SHALL use ordered, versioned migrations; a single ever-growing bootstrap SQL string SHALL NOT be the long-term migration mechanism.
- **ARCH-04-FR-008** — Migrations SHALL be idempotent where appropriate and backward-safe for rollback/promotion strategies where feasible.
- **ARCH-04-FR-009** — Append-only audit storage SHALL reject ordinary UPDATE/DELETE.
- **ARCH-04-FR-010** — Core domain entities SHALL use normalized tables/constraints/indexes where correctness and queryability require it; JSONB MAY be used for flexible metadata/version snapshots.
- **ARCH-04-FR-011** — Production startup SHALL verify schema compatibility before accepting traffic.
- **ARCH-04-FR-012** — CI SHALL test migrations and RLS against a real ephemeral PostgreSQL instance.

## 9. Detailed interaction behaviour
All components must interact through the interfaces and trust boundaries defined by this PRD. Internal convenience must never bypass Organization isolation, authorization, audit, versioning, or provider boundaries.

## 10. Business / architecture rules
- Organization is the canonical tenant/domain boundary.
- `tenant_id` may be used as the infrastructure key representing an Organization.
- Production must fail closed rather than silently falling back to Demo behaviour.
- Build artifacts are immutable; environment-specific configuration is external.

## 11. Permission rules
Infrastructure must not broaden functional permissions. Authentication, Organization membership, Board permissions, governance roles, acting capacity, confidentiality, and owner-portal isolation remain server-authoritative.

## 12. Data requirements
Every tenant-owned persisted record must carry or be unambiguously scoped to an Organization/tenant. Schema constraints and indexes must enforce correctness where practical.

## 13. API requirements
APIs must use stable contracts, server-side authorization, consistent problem responses, idempotency where required, and explicit Organization context.

## 14. Real-time / event requirements
Events must preserve Organization context, correlation metadata, authorization-safe payloads, and stable event names. Event delivery must never expose data to an unauthorized subscriber.

## 15. UX requirements
Infrastructure states that affect users—Demo Mode, integration failure, stale version, degraded availability, pending AI processing—must have understandable and non-sensitive UI states.

## 16. Accessibility requirements
Architecture must preserve WCAG 2.2 AA capability. User-facing diagnostic or error states must be keyboard and screen-reader accessible.

## 17. Error and empty states
Fail closed on missing tenant/security configuration. Do not expose SQL, stack traces, secrets, provider credentials, or inaccessible-record existence.

## 18. Edge cases
Test missing configuration, dependency outage, container restart, partial deployment, stale client, duplicate/replayed integration messages, concurrent operations, failed migrations, and interrupted CI runs as applicable.

## 19. Non-functional requirements
Security, tenant isolation, deterministic builds, maintainability, observability, reproducibility, recoverability, and least privilege are mandatory.

## 20. Analytics / telemetry
Structured logs, metrics, traces, audit events, and build metadata must correlate failures and changes without recording secrets or prohibited personal data.

## 21. Dependencies
- ARCH-03
- ARCH-06
- ARCH-09
- ARCH-12
- PRD-20
- PRD-70

## 22. Out of scope
- Database-per-tenant as the default

## 23. Acceptance criteria
- **ARCH-04-AC-001** — GIVEN Organizations A and B WHEN A queries tenant-owned data THEN no B record can be returned even in tested paths with weakened application predicates.
- **ARCH-04-AC-002** — GIVEN a clean database WHEN all migrations run THEN the expected schema is produced deterministically.
- **ARCH-04-AC-003** — GIVEN an older supported schema WHEN the new image starts THEN forward migration succeeds or traffic is refused.
- **ARCH-04-AC-004** — GIVEN an audit row WHEN ordinary update/delete SQL executes THEN PostgreSQL rejects the mutation.

## 24. Test scenarios
Automated tests must cover all acceptance criteria plus material negative/security paths. CI must execute the tests relevant to this architecture boundary.

## 25. Definition of done

items.title: Tenant fan-out: one environment over many databases or schemas
items.body:
## Problem

A product with a schema or database per tenant has to apply the same migrations to hundreds of targets. Today that means one profile per tenant and one pipeline job each, with an approval per tenant.

## Proposal

- An environment can be a unit set: a profile template plus a tenant list (static, a file, or a SQL query run with the reader at plan time). Each unit keeps its own history.
- A wave over a unit set has one gate bound to a set digest of every unit's plan; a deciding job records per-unit digests; share jobs apply subsets and refuse a unit whose plan moved since the decision; re-running continues with the units that did not finish.
- One plan comment groups identical plans across units and lists outliers.

## Done when

- Claim `tenant-wave` passes and is caught on Postgres schemas and ClickHouse databases.
- A bench in `bench/` for N tenants records fan-out time and comment size.

## Proof

Prove it with the scenario claims, rolled up (#39): the `waves` claim (a tenant part). Every part fails under BREAK=1 on its own.

Roadmap rank 17 of 30.

items.title: Tenant-scoped graph arm
items.body:
A tenant-scoped recall currently drops the graph arm entirely: graph nodes and relations carry no tenant property, so the isolation backstop excludes their results wholesale (by design — the backstop guarantees no cross-tenant fusion). The cost is that multi-tenant deployments lose graph recall and graph resurrection.

Proposed: tenant as a first-class property on nodes and relations written by the graph-sync pipeline, plus a tenant filter in `MemgraphRetriever` and the resurrection stage (alternative: a database per tenant, at the cost of connection management). Until then the arm drop is logged (added alongside the fail-closed work), not silent.

items.title: [Security/Medium]: Missing SSRF validation when connecting to external databases
UseExceptionHandler middleware can't handle exceptions from UseAuthentication middleware

labels.name: area-auth
labels.description: Includes: authentication, authorization, OAuth, OIDC, and access token validation

items.body:
### Describe the bug
When an exception is thrown from the `UseAuthentication` middleware it propagates back up the pipeline until caught by the `UseExceptionHandler` middleware which then re-executes the pipeline using the error path which then gets to the `UseAuthentication` middleware a second time but because the cached `Task` from the first call to `UseAuthentication` is returned the second time around the initial exception on the `Task` is returned as soon as it is awaited causing `UseExceptionHandler` to catch it as a secondary exception and then throw the original exception it caught.

### To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
Version 2.2.6 of ASP.NET Core
Minimal reproduction https://github.com/AquilaSands/AspNetCoreCookieErrorHandlerBug based on https://github.com/aspnet/AspNetCore.Docs/tree/master/aspnetcore/security/authentication/cookie/samples/2.x/CookieSample

1. Run the minimal repro
2. Sign in
3. Follow the 'Contact (Authentication Required)' link
4. This will cause a `CustomException` to be thrown from the custom `ValidatePrincipal()` method
5. The custom error page is not shown and you get the generic browser 500 error page

### Expected behavior
Expect the custom error page to be shown.

https://github.com/AquilaSands/AspNetCoreCookieErrorHandlerBug/blob/dc50eda4b1dfc0bbc926f00109d57b6f2193499d/log-output.txt

items.title: [Feature]: Reuse existing extractions when the same file is added to another dataset
items.body:
### Problem Statement

When the same file is added to more than one dataset, cognify runs the whole extraction pipeline again for each dataset. The LLM extraction, the embeddings, everything is paid for a second time, even when both datasets live in the same graph and vector databases and the artifacts from the first run are already sitting there. For applications where users organize shared documents into per-user or per-topic datasets this gets expensive fast, since the second run produces essentially the same nodes and edges that already exist.

### Proposed Solution

When a data item has already completed the cognify pipeline for another dataset in the same databases, link the existing artifacts to the new dataset instead of re-processing: tag the item's graph nodes and vector rows with the new dataset's NodeSet, record provenance for the new dataset, create the NodeSet anchor, and report the item as already completed. This should be opt-in through a `cross_dataset_reuse` flag on `cognify()`, defaulting to off so nothing changes for existing users. Whenever linking is not possible (backend access control enabled, adapters without tagging support, no provenance to resolve the item's nodes) the item should silently fall through to the normal full pipeline.

### Alternatives Considered

I first tried handling this at the application level by pointing several logical datasets at one shared cognee dataset, but that breaks per-dataset search scoping and permissions. I also considered copying the subgraph per dataset, but since NodeSet membership is already a list on the nodes, tagging in place is much cheaper, keeps a single copy of the knowledge, and is idempotent if the run is retried.

### Use Case

We run a document knowledge base where the same PDF is commonly added to several datasets. Today the second cognify of an already processed document costs the same as the first one. With this feature the second run becomes a merge that finishes in seconds at near zero LLM cost, and search filtered by the new dataset returns the document's knowledge as if it had been processed there.

### Implementation Ideas

I have this implemented and validated on Neo4j plus PGVector and will open a PR: a `link_data_to_dataset` module that resolves the item's existing nodes either through the relational provenance ledger or through graph-native provenance markers, a new optional `add_belongs_to_set_tags` capability on the graph and vector adapter interfaces (implemented for Neo4j, Postgres graph, PGVector and LanceDB), and a hook in the incremental pipeline path that tries the link before falling back to the full run.

### Pre-submission Checklist

- [x] I have searched existing issues to ensure this feature hasn't been requested already
- [x] I have provided a clear problem statement and proposed solution
- [x] I have described my specific use case

items.title: Consider providing an option to not re-authenticate on OpenConnection()
items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

I'm running MySqlConnector 2.4.0 against Aurora MySQL. I have a database cluster with multiple databases. Some queries span multiple databases.

Pooling is used to reduce the number of reconnects.

As mentioned in #1534, when using pooling with connection reset set to true, every call to OpenConnection() triggers a re-authentication. This behaviour is deliberate, to ensure that the selected database is in a default state after `OpenConnection()`.

However, this additional re-authentication adds additional time and load on the database server, and some systems (e.g. Aurora MySQL using IAM DB authentication) have a restriction on authentication requests/sec.

A reset of the default selected database (to that defined by the connection string) seems to me to be mostly unnecessary. In a single database scenario, the default database is not changing. In a multi-database scenario where each database represents a tenant of a multi-tenant platform, then either 
* there will be a pool for each tenant, with a database specified in the connection strings (i.e. the default database is unlikely to change)
* common pool for all tenants, where no database is specified in the connection string. In this case the default database can change but the application uses `ChangeDatabase(tenant)` as appropriate 

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I have struggled to think of why it's necessary to reset the default selected database in most cases, but I do not propose making a breaking change. Rather, a configuration option could be added to set whether a connection reset involves a re-authentication or not. 

This could be an extension of the existing ConnectionReset (expanding the options to true/false/authenticate/no-authenticate) or a new setting (ConnectionResetAuthentication = true/false)

Any risks presented by enabling this option can be easily mitigated at design-time by ensuring all queries include the database name with the table name, or by calling `ChangeDatabase() `after each `OpenConnection()`. Any new users migrating from MySql.Data are unaffected, given its default behaviour is not to re-authenticate.

Another option would be to add an argument to OpenConnection() to specify the database, i.e OpenConnection(string databaseName). If provided, this would skip re-authentication and instead internally call ChangeDatabase() before returning.

A third option is to replace the existing re-auth with an internal ChangeDatabase(), using the default database from the connection string.


**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Disabling ConnectionReset by setting it to false has been considered. This has other potential side-effects, as other session states are not cleared.

**Additional context**
I note that the MySQL API recognises the usefulness for resetting a connection with and without re-authentication, providing the `mysql_reset_connection() `and `mysql_change_user() `functions respectively.

MySql.Data does not share this same issue, as it does not reauthenticate during connection reset (but does on a change user). ref: 
https://dev.mysql.com/doc/c-api/8.4/en/mysql-reset-connection.html
https://dev.mysql.com/doc/c-api/8.4/en/mysql-change-user.html
