items.title: feat: multi-database support (two-part) — serve multiple ClickHouse databases, and make cache keys, NATS subjects, policy, and stream params database-aware

labels.name: breaking-change
labels.description: Breaking change to public API, CLI, or config

items.body:
Two-part issue requested in the #343 review (https://github.com/Wave-RF/WaveHouse/pull/343#pullrequestreview-4527311363): multi-database support would break several things at once today, because the bare table name is the identity everywhere — nothing carries the database.

WaveHouse today is single-database (`clickhouse.database`): schema discovery, ingest, structured queries, pipes, and cache invalidation all assume one database. #343's dependency resolution made the constraint visible: a cross-database read can't be version-invalidated (nothing ever bumps a cross-database table's version), so such reads are now *detected* and the cached result is TTL-capped (~10 s), and a view reading a cross-database source is unfoldable (its readers TTL-cap too). That bounds staleness but doesn't support the workload — people will reasonably want multiple databases within ClickHouse to separate concerns.

## Part 1 — support multiple databases

- Schema discovery/registry over a configured set of databases (today: one `database` string; `SchemaRegistry` keys everything by bare name).
- Ingest into database-qualified tables (worker insert path + validation).
- Structured queries and pipes reading across databases; dependency resolution keeping database-qualified names instead of dropping/flagging foreign-database tables (`discovery.ResolveTables` currently keeps only configured-database names and marks anything else external).

## Part 2 — make every identity surface database-aware, in lockstep

The write side and read side must keep building **identical** namespace keys, so all of these have to move together:

- NATS subjects: `ingest.<table>[.<scope>]`, `dlq.<table>` (`chsql.SafeEncodeNATS` tokens have no database segment).
- Cache namespaces `(table, scope)`, `VersionManager.QueryKey` folding, and the base→view cascade (`SetDependents`), all keyed by bare table name.
- The database-wide fallback version introduced in #343 (`cache.DatabaseVersionTable`, the reserved `"*"` namespace): with several databases this should become per-database versions.
- Stream/live-query URL parameters (`?table=`), policy file table keys, and the SDK surfaces that name tables.
- Schema refresh + `IsKnown` + `ClearResolvedDeps` semantics per database.

Adjacent identity work worth coordinating with: #214 (per-table policy storage / auth scopes), #235 (implement scope — the `(table, scope)` second dimension).

items.title: The Normalizer We Never Wrote: Reshaping Three Clouds' AI Telemetry in the Collector
items.body:
Every cloud that hosts AI agents emits telemetry, and every one of them emits it in a different shape. Azure AI Foundry ships log records where the model name hides under `properties.modelDeploymentName` and a content-filter block shows up as a `resultType` of `Failed`. Vertex AI hands you a `reasoning_engine_id` buried in resource labels and a free-text body you have to pattern-match to know a request was denied. If you want a single dashboard that says "here is what every agent, on every platform, for every tenant, actually did" — someone has to reconcile those shapes.

The obvious move is to write a normalizer service: a piece of code that knows all three schemas, maps them to a common model, and writes rows. We started down that road on Agent Nexus, our multi-tenant control plane for governing agents across Copilot Studio, Azure AI Foundry, and Vertex. Then we deleted the plan. The normalizer we shipped isn't code we maintain — it's an OpenTelemetry Collector configuration and a Kafka topic in between. This is how that works, and why config beat code here.

## The problem: three schemas, one dashboard

Nexus assigns each agent a live score, tracks per-tenant cost, and flags governance events — a guardrail that fired, a prompt injection that was caught, content that got filtered. All of that depends on a single fact: no matter which cloud produced an event, we need it expressed in the same vocabulary. The industry already has that vocabulary — OpenTelemetry's `gen_ai.*` semantic conventions, which name things like `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, and `gen_ai.response.finish_reason` in a provider-neutral way.

The gap is that the clouds don't emit `gen_ai.*`. They emit their own native log shapes. The reconciliation is real work, and it changes every time a provider tweaks a field. Putting that logic in a service means a deploy every time Azure renames a property. We wanted the mapping to live somewhere we could change without a code release.

## The shape: a two-stage pipeline with Kafka in the middle

The Collector runs two logical pipelines per provider. Stage one is pure intake. A raw OTLP receiver takes whatever arrives, a filter keeps only the records for that provider (`gen_ai.system == "azure.ai_foundry"`, say), and a Kafka exporter drops them onto a per-provider topic — `foundry.telemetry` or `vertex.telemetry`. That's it. No interpretation yet.

Stage two reads back off that same Kafka topic, runs the heavy transform work, and exports the normalized result to the Nexus observability API over OTLP HTTP.

```yaml
service:
  pipelines:
    logs/foundry-ingest:
      receivers:  [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, filter/foundry, batch]
      exporters:  [kafka/foundry-topic]
    logs/foundry-process:
      receivers:  [kafka/foundry]
      processors: [memory_limiter, transform/azure-monitor, transform/foundry, batch]
      exporters:  [otlphttp/nexus]
```

Splitting intake from processing across Kafka (we run Redpanda) is the decision that makes the rest tractable. Intake never blocks on transform work; a burst of telemetry lands on the topic and drains at whatever rate stage two can manage. If we change a mapping rule and want to reprocess, the raw records are still sitting on the topic. And `memory_limiter` sits at the front of both pipelines so a flood can't take the Collector down — it sheds load instead.

## The normalizer: OTTL statements, not a service

The actual reconciliation lives in `transform` processors written in OTTL — the OpenTelemetry Transformation Language. Each statement is a conditional field assignment. Here is a slice of the Azure Foundry mapping:

```yaml
transform/azure-monitor:
  log_statements:
    - context: log
      statements:
        - set(attributes["gen_ai.system"], "azure.ai_foundry")
        - set(attributes["gen_ai.request.model"],
              ParseJSON(body)["properties"]["modelDeploymentName"])
              where IsString(body) and attributes["gen_ai.request.model"] == nil
        - set(attributes["gen_ai.usage.input_tokens"],
              ParseJSON(body)["properties"]["promptTokens"])
              where IsString(body) and ParseJSON(body)["properties"]["promptTokens"] != nil
        - set(attributes["gen_ai.content.filtered"], true)
              where IsString(body) and
              IsMatch(body, "(?i).*(content_filter|jailbreak|responsibleai|blocked).*")
```

Every provider quirk we used to imagine writing `if` branches for is one `set(...) where ...` line. The Vertex mapping is its own block that digs `reasoning_engine_id` out of resource labels and pattern-matches the body for `PERMISSION_DENIED` or `no_refills` to decide a request was denied. Azure gets a separate block that reads `resultType == "Failed"` and `category == "Audit"`. When a provider changes a field name, we change one line of config — no build, no image, no code review of control flow.

## Governance as a routing decision

The part we're most pleased with is that governance isn't a downstream query — it's an attribute set during transform. If any of the guardrail signals are present, the record gets tagged into a routing tier:

```yaml
- set(attributes["gen_ai.routing.tier"], "governance") where
    attributes["gen_ai.guardrail.violated"] == true or
    attributes["gen_ai.security.injection_detected"] == true or
    attributes["gen_ai.content.filtered"] == true
```

An injection that was caught on Vertex and a content filter that fired on Foundry both come out the other end wearing the same `governance` tier tag, regardless of how their source clouds described the event. The dashboard doesn't need to know three dialects of "this was blocked" — the Collector already spoke them and translated.

## The producer: one worker, no per-cloud plumbing

The Collector processes whatever lands on the Kafka topics, but something has to produce to them from each tenant's cloud account. That's a single component — the tenant-ingest-worker. It reads platform connections out of the Connectors database, pulls each connection's credentials from Infisical under our per-tenant, two-tier credential model, and starts an ingestor per connection: a Pub/Sub subscriber for Vertex, an Event Hub reader for Foundry. Both feed the same two topics the Collector is already watching.

Its reconcile loop runs every 30 seconds. Add a new tenant connection and store its credentials, and the worker starts ingesting it on the next tick — no redeploy. That's the payoff of pushing the shape logic into config and the fan-out into one reconciling worker: onboarding a tenant is a database row and a secret, not an engineering task.

## What we'd tell another team

The instinct to write a normalizer service is strong, and for a fixed schema it might even be right. But telemetry schemas from third-party clouds are not fixed — they drift, and each drift would have been a deploy. Moving the mapping into OTTL turned "provider changed a field" from an incident into a config edit.

Two things made it hold together. First, Kafka between intake and processing: it decouples the two rates, survives bursts, and keeps raw records around for reprocessing. Second, treating governance as an attribute set at transform time rather than a query computed later — the semantics get normalized once, at the edge, and everything downstream trusts the tags.

The normalizer we never wrote is the one we don't have to maintain. When you're reconciling schemas you don't control, the least code is the code that lives in configuration.

items.title: Tested backups with defined RPO/RTO

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Situation

The platform runs PostgreSQL 16 under CloudNativePG on GKE and stores documents in object storage, but there is no defined backup strategy, no agreed recovery objectives, and — most importantly — no evidence that anything can actually be restored. CloudNativePG will take base backups and archive WAL if configured, which creates the most dangerous state in operations: backups that appear to exist and have never been proven to restore.

The stakes here are not theoretical. MediCore holds the admission, medication and nursing record for inpatients. LabConnect holds authorised pathology results a clinician is acting on. EmergencyConnect is life-critical and a data loss during an active dispatch has direct patient-safety consequences. A hospital cannot fall back to paper for a week; a multi-day outage of the clinical record is a patient-safety incident and a contractual one.

There are regulatory and commercial drivers too. NABH and NABL accreditation both expect records to be retrievable and expect the organisation to have a tested continuity arrangement. CERT-In obligations around incident handling assume the ability to recover and to preserve evidence. Every enterprise and government tender the platform will bid for asks for stated RPO and RTO with evidence of testing, and "we take nightly backups" is not an answer that survives due diligence.

Residency compounds this: an Indian tenant's backups must remain in an Indian region, so backup topology is per-country, not one global vault. Isolated per-tenant backups are also required for the dedicated-database premium tier.

Affected roles: the platform **SRE** who would today be improvising during an incident, the **hospital admin** whose continuity plan depends on a stated RTO, and the **DPO**, because a backup that outlives its retention policy is itself a DPDP Act 2023 exposure.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** platform SRE
**I want** encrypted, multi-region-safe backups of every data store with published RPO and RTO targets, and automated restore tests that prove those targets are met
**So that** the platform can recover clinical data within a committed window and can evidence that recovery capability to auditors and customers.

### Scope

**In scope**

* **PostgreSQL 16 backup** via CloudNativePG: scheduled base backups plus continuous WAL archiving to per-country object storage, enabling point-in-time recovery.
* **Object-storage backup**: versioning plus cross-zone replication within the country region for the document store from #483.
* **Published RPO/RTO targets per tier**, differentiated by criticality: EmergencyConnect and MediCore clinical stores get the tightest objectives; AdminConnect and the analytics lake get looser ones.
* **Automated restore verification**: a scheduled job that restores the most recent backup into an isolated environment, runs integrity assertions, records the measured recovery time, and fails loudly if the restore does not complete or the data fails checks.
* **Point-in-time recovery drills**, including a partial restore path for the realistic case of a single tenant's data being corrupted rather than a whole-cluster loss.
* **Per-tenant isolated backups** for dedicated-database tenants, with per-tenant encryption keys.
* **Backup retention aligned to the #480 classification policy**, including crypto-shred semantics so that a DPDP erasure is not defeated by a backup copy.
* Backup and restore metrics, freshness alerting and an SRE-facing status surface.

**Out of scope**

* Multi-region active-active failover and full disaster-recovery site orchestration — a later SRE epic; this issue delivers restorable backups and measured recovery, not automated regional failover.
* Retention policy definition itself — owned by #480; this issue implements backup expiry against those policies.
* The object-storage service, signed URLs and virus scanning — owned by #483.
* Analytics lake rebuild from source — the lake is reconstructible from OLTP by #481 backfill and is therefore backed up to a looser objective by design.
* Application-level undo, soft delete and record versioning — owned by the Audit & Traceability epic; backups are not an editing safety net.

**Recovery objectives to be ratified as part of this issue**

| Store | RPO | RTO |
|---|---|---|
| MediCore / clinical OLTP (per country) | 5 minutes | 1 hour |
| EmergencyConnect OLTP | 1 minute | 15 minutes |
| Document object store | 15 minutes | 2 hours |
| AdminConnect / billing | 1 hour | 4 hours |
| Analytics lake | 24 hours | 24 hours (rebuild from OLTP) |

---

## Recommended Solution

**PostgreSQL.** Configure CloudNativePG `ScheduledBackup` with a daily base backup and continuous WAL archiving to a per-country bucket. The 5-minute RPO for clinical OLTP is achieved by WAL archive timeout, not by backup frequency — this is the point most often got wrong. Archive success is the metric that matters: a base backup with a broken WAL archive gives an RPO of 24 hours regardless of what the schedule says, so `pg_stat_archiver.last_failed_wal` is alerted on directly. EmergencyConnect's 1-minute RPO additionally uses a synchronous replica in a second zone, so its RPO does not depend on archiving at all in the common failure case.

Backups are encrypted with a per-country KMS key; dedicated-database tenants get a per-tenant key so their backup set is cryptographically isolated and independently shreddable.

**Restore verification** is the substance of this issue. A Temporal workflow `RestoreVerificationWorkflow` runs nightly per cluster:

1. `ProvisionScratchCluster` — a CloudNativePG cluster in an isolated namespace with no network path to production and no production credentials.
2. `RestoreFromBackup` — restore the latest base backup and replay WAL to a target recovery time.
3. `AssertIntegrity` — run structural and semantic checks: expected table set present, row counts within tolerance of the source's recorded watermark, referential integrity spot-checks, a sample of encounters readable end to end, RLS policies present and enforcing.
4. `MeasureAndRecord` — write measured RTO, restored-to timestamp and achieved RPO.
5. `TeardownScratchCluster` — always runs, including on failure paths, to avoid cost and data sprawl.

Temporal is used because a restore is long-running, must be resumable, and must leave no orphaned cluster if a step dies — a plain CronJob reliably leaks scratch clusters.

```sql
CREATE TABLE backup_target (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL, country_profile text NOT NULL,
  store_kind text NOT NULL CHECK (store_kind IN ('postgres','object_store')),
  tier text NOT NULL, rpo interval NOT NULL, rto interval NOT NULL,
  kms_key_ref text NOT NULL, tenant_id uuid,   -- non-null only for dedicated-DB tenants
  UNIQUE (name, country_profile)
);

CREATE TABLE restore_verification (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY, backup_target_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES backup_target(id),
  started_at timestamptz NOT NULL, completed_at timestamptz,
  restored_to timestamptz,                  -- PITR target actually achieved
  measured_rto interval, measured_rpo interval,
  outcome text NOT NULL CHECK (outcome IN ('passed','failed','integrity_failed','timed_out')),
  integrity_findings jsonb, digest bytea    -- chained, tamper-evident
);
```

**PHI in non-prod is prohibited**, so restore verification runs in an isolated namespace that is treated as production-equivalent for access control: no engineer has standing read access, the scratch cluster is torn down within the workflow, and integrity assertions return counts and booleans rather than row content. Assertion output is explicitly checked in CI for PHI leakage.

**API surface**

```
GET  /v1/backups/targets
GET  /v1/backups/targets/{id}/status          # last backup, WAL archive lag, freshness
GET  /v1/backups/verifications?target=&from=  # verification history with measured RTO/RPO
POST /v1/backups/targets/{id}:verify          # ad-hoc restore test
POST /v1/backups/restores                     # initiate a real restore (break-glass)
GET  /v1/backups/restores/{id}
```

**Events.** Publishes `BackupCompleted`, `BackupFailed`, `RestoreVerificationPassed`, `RestoreVerificationFailed` and `RecoveryObjectiveBreached` on NATS JetStream. `RecoveryObjectiveBreached` is the one that pages: it fires when measured RPO or RTO exceeds the ratified target for that tier, which converts an abstract commitment into an operational alert.

**OpenFGA.**

```
type backup_target
  relations
    define viewer: sre or platform_admin or compliance_auditor
    define verifier: sre
    define restorer: sre_oncall           # real restores require on-call, two-person approved
```

A real production restore is destructive and requires two-person approval recorded against the `restore` record, mirroring the #480 disposal control.

**Sequencing.** Depends on CloudNativePG cluster provisioning, per-country object storage, KMS key provisioning, #483 for the document store, and #480 for retention policy alignment. Should land before the first production tenant onboards — a tenant carrying real clinical data without a proven restore path is not an acceptable position.

**Risks.** The dominant risk is silent backup failure, addressed by alerting on WAL archive failures and backup age rather than only on job exit codes, and by the nightly restore that fails loudly. Second risk is restore cost and duration growth as data grows, making the stated RTO quietly untrue — mitigated by trending measured RTO over time and alerting when it reaches 70% of the target, well before breach. Third is backup copies defeating DPDP erasure, mitigated by crypto-shred: destroying the per-patient or per-tenant data key renders backup copies unrecoverable without rewriting backup media.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a production Indian clinical PostgreSQL cluster with base backups and continuous WAL archiving configured
**When** the nightly restore verification workflow runs
**Then** a scratch cluster is provisioned in an isolated namespace, the latest backup is restored to a point-in-time target, integrity assertions pass, measured RTO is recorded and is within the 1-hour target and measured RPO within 5 minutes, `RestoreVerificationPassed` is published, the scratch cluster is torn down, and a tamper-evident digest is chained to the previous verification.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** WAL archiving to object storage has been failing for six hours because a bucket permission was changed, while base backups continue to succeed
**When** the backup monitor evaluates archive health
**Then** `BackupFailed` and `RecoveryObjectiveBreached` are published and the SRE on-call is paged with the archive failure named — not merely a generic "backup unhealthy" — the effective RPO is reported as the true degraded figure rather than the target, the nightly restore verification runs anyway and records `integrity_failed` or a restored-to timestamp behind target, and the target's status surface shows the store as out of objective until archiving recovers.

### Edge Cases

* A restore verification exceeds its time budget — the workflow times out, records `timed_out` with the elapsed duration, still tears down the scratch cluster, and pages rather than silently retrying forever.
* Measured RTO trends upward with data growth and reaches 70% of target — a warning fires ahead of any breach, prompting a capacity or strategy review.
* A single tenant's data is corrupted by application error while the cluster is otherwise healthy — the partial restore path recovers that tenant into a scratch cluster and re-imports only their rows under RLS, without a whole-cluster rollback affecting other tenants.
* A DPDP erasure was executed for a patient after the most recent base backup — restoring that backup must not resurrect the erased data; the crypto-shred means their records are unrecoverable in the restored copy, and the verification asserts this explicitly.
* A dedicated-database tenant's backup is attempted with the shared country key — the operation fails rather than succeeding with the wrong key, since key isolation is the product promise for that tier.
* Object storage returns partial or throttled reads mid-restore — the restore retries with backoff and either completes or fails cleanly; a half-restored cluster is never reported as passed.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team’s agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** Every data store has an encrypted backup with a ratified RPO and RTO, and a nightly automated restore proves those objectives are actually met rather than merely configured.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** The platform can answer enterprise and government continuity due-diligence with measured evidence, supports NABH and NABL expectations for record retrievability, and can onboard clinical tenants with a defensible recovery position.
* **Success metric or validation method:** Restore verification pass rate ≥98% over any rolling 30-day window, with any failure triaged within one business day; measured RTO for clinical OLTP under 1 hour and measured RPO under 5 minutes on 100% of passing verifications; WAL archive failure alerting within 5 minutes of first failure; a quarterly full disaster-recovery game day performed against a production-scale dataset with the measured recovery time recorded and published; zero DPDP-erased records resurrected by any verified restore.
* **Monitoring period:** Continuous. Verification runs nightly and its result is a standing SRE dashboard item; the RTO trend is reviewed monthly against the 70% early-warning threshold.

---

## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---

## Exceptions

**Guardrail:** Accessibility and User Journey — keyboard navigation, focus behaviour, WCAG level, cross-device support.
**Reason:** The deliverable is backup configuration, a Temporal verification workflow and an SRE-facing API. There is no end-user interface; the SRE status surface is a dashboard built in the Observability epic.
**Alternative validation:** The status and verification APIs are contract-tested for empty (no verifications yet), in-progress, passed and failed states, including the degraded-RPO representation, so the dashboard can render honestly.
**Residual risk:** Low. SREs consume this through alerting and API until the dashboard lands.
**Approved by:** SRE lead.

**Guardrail:** Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
**Reason:** There is no browser journey. The equivalent critical journey is restore itself.
**Alternative validation:** The nightly restore verification workflow *is* the end-to-end test, executed continuously against real backups rather than a fixture, plus a quarterly full disaster-recovery game day at production scale.
**Residual risk:** Low; this is stronger coverage than a synthetic E2E suite would provide for this capability.
**Approved by:** SRE lead.

items.title: [Question]:How to implement multi tenant solutions?
items.body:
### Do you need to ask a question?

- [x] I have searched the existing question and discussions and this question is not already answered.
- [ ] I believe this is a legitimate question, not just a bug or feature request.

### Your Question


I'm exploring using LightRAG + POSTGRES for storage in a multi-tenant application and am running into some challenges with managing data isolation between tenants.
What I've Considered
I noticed the workspace isolation option, which seems useful for defining different environments. However, it feels difficult to dynamically switch this configuration at runtime for each incoming API request. The persistence of the connection pools seems to prevent a clean switch from one tenant's database/schema to another's on a per-request basis.

My Question
Is there a recommended or existing way to manage a multi-tenant setup with LightRAG that I might be missing?

For example, is there a way to:

Dynamically pass tenant-specific database postgres credentials/configurations to the LightRAG or other components for each operation? OR use a single database with workspace isolations that can easily be modified during run time...


Any guidance or best practices you could share on this would be greatly appreciated. Thank you for the fantastic library!

### Additional Context

_No response_

items.title: Audit findings — security, concurrency, reliability, scalability

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Maintainer needs to evaluate this issue

items.body:
Audit of the implementation against the fourteen failure modes the design set out to prevent. Each finding was checked against the code, not against the design doc's claims about the code. **Thirteen of the fourteen hold**; the sub-issues below are what does not, plus the latent items worth an explicit decision before they become real.

Verified on branch `main` at `539c3d7`. `npm run typecheck` passes.

Source: `.scratch/access-control/issues/audit-findings.md`

### Findings (severity order)

| # | Finding | Severity | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F1 | A retried refresh revokes the user's entire session family | high | ready-for-agent |
| F2 | Nothing stops a read replica from restoring revoked access | medium (latent) | needs-triage |
| F3 | The version-skew CI gate is a no-op unless the deploy pipeline sets one variable | medium | needs-info |
| F4 | Login against an unknown tenant slug is neither throttled nor audited | low | ready-for-agent |
| F5 | The shard-key cache is never invalidated | informational | wontfix |

### What was checked and found sound

Listed so a later reader knows these were verified against code rather than assumed, and does not re-audit them.

| Failure mode | Where it is handled |
| --- | --- |
| Connection pooling leaks | `tenant-database.ts:105` — `BEGIN` + `set_config(..., true)` per transaction, never a session-level `SET`. Every background job that takes a raw pool does the same with its own sweep setting. RLS is `ENABLE` **and** `FORCE` on every tenant-owned table; `app` is explicitly `NOBYPASSRLS` (`002_app_role.sql:21`). |
| Confused deputy | `payroll.controller.ts` — `InternalTokenGuard` then `AuthzGuard`. The second re-evaluates the acting user's own snapshot and knows nothing about the caller (§8.3 rule 5). |
| Stolen token reuse | Opaque refresh tokens, stored as `sha256` only, rotated in one transaction, with family-wide revocation on replay. |
| Insider / support access | `013_support_grants.sql` — ≤4 hours, one tenant, reason and ticket required, `approved_by <> requested_by` enforced by the database. No bypass role exists. |
| Token bloat and staleness | `token-signer.ts:57` — `iss/sub/tid/sid/typ/aud/iat/exp/jti` and nothing else (D4). Even the support token omits the access level. |
| Concurrent admin edits | `roles.repository.ts:198` — compare-and-set on `version`; the controller makes the version mandatory, so there is no implicit-overwrite path. |
| Dropped invalidation events | `snapshot-cache.ts:77` — both cached tiers re-check version and epoch. Pub/sub is the optimisation; the counters are the guarantee (N4 runs with pub/sub off). |
| Temporal expiry | Two sweepers schedule a rebuild a second after each stated expiry; correctness does not depend on them, only timeliness. |
| Cache stampede | Single-flight `inflight` map plus ±20% jitter on every TTL. |
| Redis / auth outage | Circuit breaker, longer degraded TTL, stale serving up to a ceiling, then **503** rather than 403. |
| Org tree load | Materialized path with a `text_pattern_ops` prefix index; no recursive CTE on the hot path. |

items.title: Wayfinder Map: TRAME V1 Clean-Slate Architecture & Implementation Roadmap
items.body:
## Destination

Deliver **TRAME V1** (*Tabletop Rules, Actors, Maps & Encounters*): a single-binary Rust (`Axum` + `Tokio` + `SQLx`) + shared WebAssembly (`trame-engine`) + `PixiJS v8` Virtual Tabletop with native MCP parity, generic `GameSystemPack` + built-in D&D 5e (SRD 5.1), 3-tier collaborative Markdown notes (`yrs` CRDT + Obsidian 3-way merge), and scale-to-zero Cloud Run / Neon / R2 hosting.

## Notes

- **Local workflow**: Docker Compose + root `Makefile` (`make up`, `make test`, `make lint`, `make wasm`).
- **Skills**: `wayfinder`, `to-tickets`, `tdd`, `codebase-design`, `domain-modeling`.
- **Execution Split**:
  - **Critical Path Foundations (`F1`–`F5`, label `ready-for-human` + `wayfinder:task`)**: Owned and implemented directly by the Primary Architect Agent (Claude Opus / Cursor) to establish rock-solid Rust/WASM traits, concurrency actors, shaders, and security boundaries.
  - **Vertical Feature Slices (`E1`–`E8`, label `ready-for-agent`)**: Delegated to **Gemini 3.8 Flash via EPURE** (`/epure plan` -> `/epure approve`) once their blocking foundation seam is merged and tested.

## Decisions so far

- [Architecture & Stack Selection](https://github.com/Hartorn-Inc/trame/blob/dev/ARCHITECTURE.md): Rust single-binary (`trame-server`) + shared Rust/WASM (`trame-engine`) + React 19 / PixiJS v8 (`packages/web`).
- [Virtual Table & Spatial Spec](https://github.com/Hartorn-Inc/trame/blob/dev/docs/specs/01-TABLE-SPEC.md): Exploration (120ms tick + `Spacebar` freeze) vs. Turn-by-Turn modes, 2.5D BVH raycasting, 3-layer Fog of War, 4 AoE discretization modes, and 50-action GM Undo ring buffer.
- [Generic Game Engine & D&D 5e Spec](https://github.com/Hartorn-Inc/trame/blob/dev/docs/specs/02-GAME-ENGINE-AND-DND5E.md): Declarative `GameSystemPack`, `derivedDAG` formulas, 5-phase `ActiveEffect` pipeline (`BASE -> ADD -> MULTIPLY -> OVERRIDE -> CLAMP`), and field-level `VisibilityTier`.
- [Native MCP & Collaborative Notes Spec](https://github.com/Hartorn-Inc/trame/blob/dev/docs/specs/03-MCP-AND-NOTES-SPEC.md): 100% `TrameCommand` parity via MCP, `MCP Staging Mode` ghost preview, `yrs` CRDT collaborative wiki, `:::dm` / `:::handout` blocks, and 3-way Obsidian sync.
- [Runtime & Scale-to-Zero Hosting Spec](https://github.com/Hartorn-Inc/trame/blob/dev/docs/specs/04-RUNTIME-AND-DEDICATED-HOSTING.md): In-memory `TableRoomActor`, hybrid WAL + write-behind persistence, 15m `Idle-Lease`, `ChaCha20Rng` dice, R2 presigned URLs, and `.trame` portable archives.

## Not yet specified

- Post-V1 community `GameSystemPack` registry & Call of Cthulhu 7e pack.
- WebRTC voice/video overlay integration (external Discord/LiveKit bridge).

## Out of scope

- 3D WebGL model terrain / miniature rendering (TRAME is strictly 2D top-down with 2.5D elevation attributes).
- Multi-tenant SaaS shared database (TRAME uses dedicated micro-instances per group).

items.title: Production mode never runs the runtime's boot-time DDL, so a production DB drifts from a development one (search_vector, dazzle_files.uploaded_by, _dazzle_usage_events)
items.body:
## What we found

On Dazzle v0.123.0 (`b29c0258`), with `DAZZLE_ENV=production` and the schema managed by the Alembic chain (release phase runs `dazzle db upgrade head`), diffing production's tables and columns against a database built from nothing to the same Alembic head (`dazzle db upgrade head` on an empty DB, then the app booted once in development mode) shows objects that exist only where a development boot has happened:

| Object | Created by | On a production-mode DB |
|---|---|---|
| `CohortAssessment.search_vector` (generated tsvector) + its GIN index | `dazzle/http/runtime/search_schema.py` (`ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS search_vector …`, run after `metadata.create_all`) | missing |
| `dazzle_files.uploaded_by` | `dazzle/http/runtime/file_storage.py:352` (`ALTER TABLE dazzle_files ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS uploaded_by TEXT`) | missing |
| `_dazzle_usage_events` (+ indexes) | `dazzle/http/runtime/usage_signal.py:45` (`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`) | missing |
| `_dazzle_events`, `_dazzle_dlq`, `_dazzle_consumer_offsets`, `devices` | runtime / `framework_tables.py` | present (created earlier, before we switched to production mode) |

So a DSL `search:` spec, the file store's uploader column and the usage signal depend on DDL that only a development-mode boot applies. Production mode (rightly) runs no boot-time DDL, and nothing in the Alembic chain (`0001_framework_baseline` … `0027_two_factor_restore`) creates these objects, so a production database silently lacks them for ever. The same class of drift bit this project in May (ADR-0010: `create_all` never added columns).

## What we would like

One of:

1. Framework Alembic migrations for everything the runtime otherwise creates at boot (`_dazzle_usage_events`, `dazzle_files.uploaded_by`, the event/dlq/offset tables, `devices`), so a production-mode DB at head has them; and for search, a migration helper the project can call (or `dazzle db upgrade` applying `build_search_index_ddl` for the spec's `search:` entities as a post-upgrade step, since the generated column's expression comes from the DSL).
2. Or a `dazzle db sync-runtime-schema` command that applies exactly the runtime's idempotent `IF NOT EXISTS` DDL to a target DB, callable from a release phase.

Either way a `dazzle db verify` (or `dazzle db check`) that reports "runtime objects missing on this DB" would let a release gate catch it.

## How we see it today

Project-side we now run a normaliser after every deploy (`pipeline/db/normalise.py` in cyfutureuk/aegismark) that diffs prod's `information_schema.columns` against a head-migrated reference DB; it is what reported the three rows above. Happy to test a fix on our pin bump.

items.title: Track Engram → Spanner compatibility execution and sign-off
items.body:
## Current scope decision — 2026-10-08: disposable experiments

Stakeholder explicitly excludes historical-data migration, old-pack identity conversion and cross-version historical upgrade work from ALL current goals. Do not spend analysis/implementation/review effort on migration or treat it as a completion blocker. Focus on actual Engram ingestion, ontology projection and retrieval on real Spanner using disposable data. In-run revision history and same-pack retry/recovery remain covered. Existing migration-only scenarios/tickets stay deferred, never falsely passed or closed. Goal Three is still unstarted pending approval.

Persisted goal-wide scope and verification standard: https://github.com/arunmenon/Engram/blob/9294db7/docs/review/spanner-compatibility/2026-10-08-small-goal-inventory.md . This scope decision overrides historical migration acceptance text below for current goal execution.

---

## Current agreed context — 2026-10-07

**Scope:** Real-Spanner compatibility remains unsigned: baseline 65 rows is separate from planned composition/tenant extensions and feature acceptance.

**Required proof:** Maintain all scenario assertions, publish redacted evidence, resolve failures/partial/blockers and verify tenant-bound handshake, ingestion, workers, both retrieval paths and operations.

**Shared decisions:** Core is mandatory. Optional memory/user/domain capabilities compose through declared dependencies, without pairwise hardcoded flows. Authenticated tenant identity resolves its authorized Spanner database and pack bundle; processing and retrieval use that same context. Never infer authorization from agent_id, caller-chosen database or artifact IDs.

**Tracking and status:** Parent #34 holds the reconciled six-bucket scope; #35/#42 own composition/capability controls, #43 tenant routing, #39 exact conformance and #41 real-Spanner execution. This is a scope/context reconciliation, not a fresh runtime verification. The issue remains open; historical reproductions below retain their original revision, backend and run scope. Historical memory probes are diagnostic evidence, not cloud acceptance. No Redis/Neo4j runners or cross-backend migration are required. Pinned documentation links below are historical published snapshots; newer local reports/run artifacts remain unpublished unless explicitly linked to a published revision.

---

Track Engram’s end-to-end compatibility with real Google Cloud Spanner. This is the execution and sign-off umbrella; #34 owns reusable ontology-pack integration and its implementation slices. Existing defects remain linked rather than duplicated or reparented.

## Baseline and evidence

Current baseline: **65 scenarios: 14 passed, 36 failed, 13 not fully executed, 2 blocked. No compatibility sign-off.** `not_run` includes partial execution whose complete assertions remain open. These are scenario counts, not unique defect counts. The 36 failed scenarios map to existing defects across #4–#33; local fixes and scoped reviews do not close cloud scenarios without reruns.

- [Scenario matrix](https://github.com/arunmenon/Engram/blob/5e9c883/docs/review/spanner-compatibility/scenarios.csv)
- [Execution ledger](https://github.com/arunmenon/Engram/blob/5e9c883/docs/review/spanner-compatibility/runs.jsonl)
- [Findings](https://github.com/arunmenon/Engram/blob/5e9c883/docs/review/spanner-compatibility/findings.md)
- [Compatibility and implementation plan](https://github.com/arunmenon/Engram/blob/5e9c883/docs/review/2026-10-06-spanner-compatibility-plan.md)

The published links are immutable baseline snapshots. Current working records live at the same repository paths. Raw `runs/` artifacts are currently local and unpublished; a recorded evidence path is not a public artifact link. Publish reviewable, redacted evidence before final sign-off.

## Execution rules

- Exercise Engram APIs, workers, admin tools and retrieval against real Spanner. No Redis or Neo4j runners; memory tests cannot substitute for cloud acceptance.
- Track every run in the execution ledger before starting. Record scenario IDs, source revision and working diff, configuration, resource scope, observations, linked defects, cleanup and final outcomes. Keep credentials out of evidence.
- Use the authorized disposable databases `engram` and `engram-compat-target` on `portiq-mvp/engram-experiment`; preserve databases and schema. Serialize destructive fixture resets and record their scope.
- Classify failures as shared Engram engine, Engram Spanner adapter, test harness or environment. Link each confirmed product defect and rerun affected scenarios after fixes.
- Test ontology updates and rebuilt-graph cutover within Spanner while preserving the ledger. Redis-to-Spanner migration is outside scope.
- Keep this checklist and the CSV synchronized. Check a scenario only when all its listed assertions have passed. Track partial assertions in subchecks; do not promote partial results to passes.

## Full baseline checklist

### Failed — 36

- [ ] **BOOT-01** — startup; `API lifespan + worker CLI`. Verify: all five ports Spanner; independent processes share data; shutdown/clients. Defects: #26. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-04`.
- [ ] **BOOT-03** — schema; `API/worker startup`. Verify: missing/wrong database/schema/dimensions/index readiness; creation disabled. Defects: #23. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-04`.
- [ ] **ING-01** — single; `POST /v1/events`. Verify: valid/invalid fields/payload; naive/aware/future time; namespaces; trusted ID. Defects: #4, #5, #15. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-01`.
- [ ] **ING-02** — batch; `POST /v1/events/batch`. Verify: empty/max/max+1; mixed outcomes; duplicate/conflicting IDs; indices. Defects: #4, #5. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-07`.
- [ ] **ING-03** — transport; `single/batch/import`. Verify: gzip truncation/CRC/trailing/multiple members; byte/decoded size; timeout. Defects: #16. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-01`.
- [ ] **ING-04** — idempotence; `single/batch/import retry`. Verify: uncertain commit; concurrent same ID; changed contents; committed prefix. Defects: #28. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-06`.
- [ ] **HOOK-03** — webhook boundary; `signed webhook routes`. Verify: signature/secret/unsupported source; changed delivery redelivery; malformed nested shape; timestamp; fanout partial writes; stalled body. Defects: #4, #17. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-01`.
- [ ] **LED-01** — JSON; `ingest → worker reads`. Verify: nested float tags/null/bool/list/unicode/datetime; lossless round-trip. Defects: #27. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-04`.

- [ ] **SUB-02** — retries; `actual worker loops`. Verify: live transient/permanent failure; bounded backoff; DLQ; pending beyond one page; partial ACK. Defects: #14. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-04`.
- [ ] **SUB-03** — restart; `worker stop/kill/restart`. Verify: crash before/after graph write/ACK; orphan pagination; surviving replica; stop during retry. Defects: #14, #19. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-02`.

- [ ] **PEXT-02** — pack evidence; `pack_extraction CLI loop`. Verify: authoritative node/link preservation; known-item caps; missing endpoints; extraction first. Defects: #10. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-05`.
- [ ] **MEM-01** — context; `GET /v1/context/{session_id}`. Verify: empty/missing; pages/ties; access updates; time budget; evidence. Defects: #31, #32. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-07`.
- [ ] **MEM-02** — lineage; `GET /v1/nodes/{node_id}/lineage`. Verify: dynamic labels/GQL keys; cyclic branching graph; depth/node bounds; missing parent. Defects: #24. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-04`.

- [ ] **MEM-05** — pagination/timeouts; `context/lineage/subgraph APIs`. Verify: tie/cursor pages; max_nodes/depth/time; cancellation including SDK thread completion. Defects: #24, #31, #32. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-07`.
- [ ] **ART-03** — admission; `POST /v1/query/artifacts`. Verify: trusted/untrusted/superseded/reversed/proposed/rejected/alternate valid route. Defects: #7. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-02`.
- [ ] **ART-04** — completeness; `POST /v1/query/artifacts`. Verify: call/scan/neighbor budget; confirmed link unseen; unknown vs absent; empty answer. Defects: #6. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-02`.
- [ ] **ONT-02** — version upgrade; `projection startup reconcile`. Verify: initial/additive/mapping/breaking/version refusal; failed replay restart. Defects: #11. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-04`.

items.title: feat(notifications): introduce a full notifications bus with triggers, digests and notifiers

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Use case

OpenAEV has no general-purpose notification system today: the only existing feature is the scenario score-degradation email rule (`NotificationRule`), which is hardcoded to a single trigger type and a single delivery channel. Users cannot subscribe to platform events (scenario created, finding updated, endpoint deleted, ...), cannot receive periodic digests, and there is no in-app notification feed, no webhook integration and no notification bell.

OpenCTI has a full notifications engine (triggers, digests, notifiers) that has proven its model. This issue is about porting that model to OpenAEV.

## Proposed solution

Introduce a full notifications bus / engine modeled on OpenCTI:

### Triggers (self-service)

- **Live triggers**: subscribe to create / update / delete events on a curated catalog of resource types (scenario, simulation, inject, finding, endpoint, asset group, team, player, payload, vulnerability, security platform, document, challenge), optionally refined by a filter group (same filter semantics and builder as the /search endpoints) or scoped to a single entity (instance triggers).
- **Digest triggers**: aggregate the events of composed live triggers over a period (hour / day / week / month) and deliver one aggregated notification at a configured UTC time.
- Recipients default to the trigger owner; administrators can target other users or groups (group recipients fan out to their members).

### Engine

- Live stage: consumes the platform-wide entity lifecycle events already published by `ModelBaseListener` (the same bus feeding SSE), matches them against cached live triggers per tenant, re-checks filter groups against the database (JPA Specification, identical semantics to /search), records one outbox row per (trigger, user) match in a new `notification_events` table (the digest source, equivalent to OpenCTI's stream.notification) and dispatches immediately.
- Digest stage: a Quartz job evaluates digest firing times every minute (OpenCTI isTimeTrigger semantics) and replays the outbox window per recipient.
- Retention: a daily job purges outbox rows older than the largest digest period.

### Notifiers (delivery channels)

- **User interface**: persisted per-user `notifications` rows + live SSE delivery scoped to the owner (notification bell with unread badge in the top bar, notifications page with mark read / delete).
- **Email**: FreeMarker subject/body templates (default template provided), delivered through the existing tenant-aware MailingService.
- **Webhook**: templated HTTP call (URL, verb, headers, FreeMarker body template, default JSON payload).
- Built-in notifiers ("User interface", "Default mailer") seeded per tenant, read-only; custom notifiers managed in Settings > Notifiers (tenant settings capability) with a test endpoint sending a sample notification through the real pipeline.

### Frontend

- Notification bell with live unread badge in the top bar.
- Profile > Notifications: paginated feed with live/digest rendering, mark read/unread, delete, mark all as read.
- Profile > Triggers: self-service management of live and digest triggers with the queryable filter builder.
- Settings > Notifiers: admin CRUD with type-specific forms and test dialog.
- Instance-trigger subscription bell on the scenario header (one click subscribes to all events of that scenario).

## Documented v1 limitations / follow-ups

- Filtered triggers do not fire on deletions (the row is gone at evaluation time); unfiltered and instance triggers do.
- Update events match the current state only (no OpenCTI-style reverse-patch "newly visible / no longer visible" translation).
- The legacy scenario score-degradation `NotificationRule` is left untouched; folding it into the new engine as a dedicated trigger type is a follow-up.
- Email theming (tenant logo / white-mark) for the default notification template is a follow-up.

items.body:
## Summary

Implement comprehensive multi-tenancy support for Encina, enabling SaaS applications to serve multiple tenants with proper data isolation.

## Motivation

Multi-tenancy is one of the most requested features for modern SaaS applications. According to community research, this is a critical capability that ABP Framework provides but most mediator libraries lack.

## Proposed Solution

### New Package: `Encina.MultiTenancy`

#### Core Interfaces

```csharp
public interface ITenantContext
{
    TenantId? CurrentTenantId { get; }
    string? CurrentTenantName { get; }
    bool IsHost { get; } // Host = no tenant context
}

public interface IMultiTenant
{
    TenantId TenantId { get; }
}

public interface ITenantResolver
{
    Task<TenantId?> ResolveAsync(CancellationToken ct = default);
}
```

#### Tenant Resolution Strategies

```csharp
public enum TenantResolutionStrategy
{
    Header,        // X-Tenant-Id header
    Subdomain,     // tenant.example.com
    QueryString,   // ?tenantId=xxx
    Route,         // /tenants/{tenantId}/...
    Claim,         // JWT claim
    Cookie,        // Cookie-based
    Custom         // User-defined
}
```

#### Data Isolation Levels

```csharp
public enum DataIsolationLevel
{
    RowLevel,      // Same database, TenantId column filter
    Schema,        // Same database, separate schemas
    Database       // Separate database per tenant
}
```

#### Configuration API

```csharp
services.AddEncinaMultiTenancy(config => {
    config.Strategy = TenantResolutionStrategy.Header;
    config.HeaderName = "X-Tenant-Id";
    config.IsolationLevel = DataIsolationLevel.RowLevel;
    config.DefaultTenantId = null; // null = require tenant
});
```

#### Pipeline Integration

```csharp
// Automatic behavior that sets tenant context
public class TenantContextPipelineBehavior<TRequest, TResponse>
    : IPipelineBehavior<TRequest, TResponse>
```

### EF Core Integration

- `TenantQueryFilter` - Automatic query filter by TenantId
- `ITenantConnectionStringResolver` - Connection string per tenant
- `TenantSchemaResolver` - Schema per tenant

## Alternatives Considered

1. **ABP Framework's multi-tenancy module**: ABP provides mature multi-tenancy support, but it's tightly coupled to ABP's module system, entity base classes, and infrastructure. Encina's approach is lightweight and integrates with existing entities.

2. **Finbuckle.MultiTenant**: This library offers similar functionality with multiple resolution strategies, but it's designed for ASP.NET Core middleware only. Encina's approach integrates with the CQRS pipeline and domain layer, not just HTTP requests.

3. **Manual TenantId filtering in repositories**: Requiring developers to add `Where(x => x.TenantId == current)` to every query, but this is error-prone, easy to forget, and doesn't work for schema or database isolation strategies.

## Affected Packages

- [x] Encina (core)
- [x] Encina.AspNetCore
- [x] Encina.EntityFrameworkCore
- [x] Encina.Dapper.*
- [x] Encina.ADO.*
- [x] Encina.MongoDB
- [ ] Encina.Messaging
- [ ] Encina.Caching.*
- [x] Other: `Encina.MultiTenancy` (new package)

## Additional Context

### Tasks

- [ ] Design `ITenantContext` and related interfaces
- [ ] Implement tenant resolution strategies
- [ ] Create `TenantContextPipelineBehavior`
- [ ] Implement Row-Level Security with EF Core query filters
- [ ] Implement Schema-per-tenant isolation
- [ ] Implement Database-per-tenant isolation
- [ ] Add ASP.NET Core middleware for tenant resolution
- [ ] Create tenant management abstractions (`ITenantStore`)
- [ ] Add comprehensive tests
- [ ] Documentation

### References

- [ABP Multi-Tenancy](https://abp.io/architecture/multi-tenancy)
- [Multi-Tenant Applications with EF Core - Milan Jovanović](https://www.milanjovanovic.tech/blog/multi-tenant-applications-with-ef-core)
- [PostgreSQL Row Level Security demo](https://github.com/PeterKneale/micro-saas)

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Support for all three isolation levels
- [ ] Support for at least 4 resolution strategies
- [ ] Automatic tenant filtering in queries
- [ ] Integration with existing `IRequestContext`
- [ ] Zero performance overhead when multi-tenancy is disabled

### Related Issues

- #359 - Module Data Isolation
- #361 - Feature Flag Integration


## Cross-Cutting Integration

> Per CLAUDE.md Cross-Cutting Integration Rule: Every new feature MUST be evaluated against ALL 12 transversal functions.
> Mark each: ✅ Included in this feature | ⏭️ Deferred (separate issue) | ❌ N/A (explain why)

| # | Function | Status | Notes |
|---|----------|--------|-------|
| 1 | **Caching** | ⏭️ Deferred | Per-tenant cache isolation |
| 2 | **OpenTelemetry** | ✅ Included | Tenant context in all traces |
| 3 | **Structured Logging** | ✅ Included | TenantId in all log entries |
| 4 | **Health Checks** | ⏭️ Deferred | Per-tenant health monitoring |
| 5 | **Validation** | ✅ Included | Tenant resolution validation |
| 6 | **Resilience** | ⏭️ Deferred | Per-tenant circuit breakers |
| 7 | **Distributed Locks** | ⏭️ Deferred | Tenant-scoped lock keys |
| 8 | **Transactions** | ⏭️ Deferred | Tenant context in transactions |
| 9 | **Idempotency** | ⏭️ Deferred | Tenant-scoped idempotency keys |
| 10 | **Multi-Tenancy** | ✅ Included | Multi-tenancy IS this feature |
